articles.title: Record El Niño? Depends who’s counting
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Britain’s Met Office says this year’s El Niño is “unprecedented.” Japan’s weather agency has called it the strongest ever observed. US forecasters say…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON — Britain’s Met Office says this year’s El Niño is “unprecedented.” Japan’s weather agency has called it the strongest ever observed. US forecasters say it still trails the biggest events in its record books. How can they all be right? The answer lies in how they measure El Niño’s strength, with meteorological agencies using different methods to assess the climate phenomenon that make direct comparisons difficult. “By any measure, we are looking at a very strong El Niño,” climate scientist Emily Becker of the University of Miami told AFP, adding that only once it is over will scientists be able to assess how big it is and “where it fits in the context of history.” Natural climate driver The Pacific Ocean’s El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the planet’s main natural climate driver. Normally, trade winds blow east to west along the equator, pushing warm water from South America toward Asia, while cold water rises from the depths to replace it. READ: El Niño affects over 451,000 people in PH – NDRRMC El Niños, which occur every two to seven years on average and last nine to 12 months, disrupt this pattern. The trade winds weaken and warm water is pushed back east toward the Americas. That shift in where ocean heat is released into the atmosphere ripples across global weather, making some regions cooler and wetter and others hotter and drier. In describing the El Niño as unprecedented, the Met Office points to raw temperatures in the Pacific. “Our observations confirm that sea-surface temperatures in the central equatorial Pacific have now surpassed levels recorded during previous El Niño events,” it said in a statement to AFP. But absolute temperatures are just one way of measuring El Niño’s strength. Agencies also look at anomalies — how far temperatures rise above a historic baseline — to assess the event. The Japan Meteorological Agency last week declared this El Niño the strongest on record based on how far sea surface temperatures were above normal in the Niño3 region of the eastern Pacific. By its count, the event beat 1997 in observations going back to 1949. The US watches a neighboring box, Niño3.4, in the east-central Pacific. It declares an El Niño when temperatures there run at least 0.5C above normal and the atmosphere responds, weakening the trade winds and shifting tropical rainfall eastward. This process is known as “ocean-atmosphere coupling.” Accounting for climate change How “normal” is defined has been a matter of significant debate. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and other agencies including the UN’s World Meteorological Organization long used the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), which compares temperatures to a 30-year average that is updated every five years, so that the baseline keeps pace with a warming climate. READ: Super El Niño demands urgent, science-based governance But with climate change speeding up and warming oceans worldwide, NOAA now uses the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), and the WMO is in the process of switching. RONI also relies on a 30-year average but goes on to measure how warm or cool the east-central Pacific is compared to the rest of the tropical ocean, because it is that difference that drives the weather impacts we care about. “We were finding a mismatch between the temperature of the tropical Pacific and the impacts,” said Becker about the old index. La Niña years, when the central and eastern tropical Pacific is cooler than normal, were producing stronger effects than their rating suggested, and El Niños weaker ones. NOAA projects this El Niño will be the strongest in its records, which go back to 1950, if the three-month average RONI anomaly reaches 2.5C or higher, a level that would put it above the 1982-83, 2015-16, and 1997-98 events. The chances are rated “high,” but not yet certain. “Regardless of where we’re ranking or how we’re measuring this event, it’s an incredible opportunity to study and understand this very powerful phenomenon in the context of a warming world,” said Becker. /dl

articles.title: [OPINION] Stop dividing the healthcare pie. Make it bigger.
articles.summary: If medical associations are advocating more equitable public financing, could they also propose reducing or waiving professional fees for indigent patients receiving publicly funded treatment?

blocks.text: When healthcare professionals call for more funding for PhilHealth, I agree. When they demand that money be redirected from the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) program, I also understand their reasoning. Healthcare should be a right, not a political favor.

Recently, more than 70 health organizations urged Congress to increase PhilHealth’s proposed 2027 allocation from approximately P74 billion to P244 billion, redirect MAIFIP funding, and release some P311 billion in withheld health-related earmarks. These are substantive proposals addressing genuine financing problems.

But while I agree with the advocates’ objectives, I question whether their proposed strategy adequately addresses Philippine political realities, the practical transition for patients, and the longer-term challenge of financing universal healthcare. The disagreement is not about where we want healthcare to go. It is about how we get there.

MAIFIP exists within a political system where elected officials are expected to provide immediate, visible assistance to constituents. For a legislator, helping a patient settle a P300,000 hospital bill may carry considerably more political value than supporting an increase in PhilHealth’s budget. We may condemn this as patronage, but political incentives do not disappear simply because a better institutional arrangement exists.

Nor can we ignore patients who currently depend on MAIFIP. Abruptly removing assistance without ensuring that PhilHealth can reliably cover the same needs risks leaving vulnerable Filipinos worse off. A credible transition would establish automatic eligibility, predictable benefits, transparent processing, and clear responsibility for patients whose costs remain uncovered. Political reform is about building an alternative that works well enough to replace the current system. (READ: Here’s PhilHealth timeline for expected benefit expansion until 2028)

There is another uncomfortable question for my fellow physicians. While we debate government allocations, have we sufficiently examined the financial responsibilities of healthcare providers? If medical associations are advocating more equitable public financing, could they also propose reducing or waiving professional fees for indigent patients receiving publicly funded treatment? Could specialists accept standardized fees for certain procedures?

Healthcare spending eventually becomes somebody’s revenue: hospitals, pharmaceutical companies, medical suppliers, laboratories, and physicians. If affordability is our objective, every participant in that economic chain deserves scrutiny. Reform should involve shared responsibility, ensuring that additional public financing translates into more affordable care rather than higher payments throughout the system.

Passing ambitious legislation is not the same as delivering accessible and affordable healthcare. The Universal Health Care Act established an important framework, yet Filipinos continue to experience substantial out-of-pocket expenses, fragmented services, and uncertainty about what their insurance covers.

Recovering earmarked revenues is necessary, but how quickly can PhilHealth convert additional financing into dependable benefits? Even if the proposed funding gap were closed, would the institutional capacity exist to deliver all promised services effectively? More importantly, as the population ages and advanced treatments become more expensive, we cannot rely indefinitely on reallocating existing government resources. We need to expand the economic capacity that makes universal healthcare financially sustainable.

Consider the Philippine business process outsourcing industry. In 2025, the IT-BPM sector generated more than $40 billion in export revenues, compared with approximately $8 billion appropriated across the government’s health sector for 2026. One Philippine export industry generates more than five times the government’s annual healthcare allocation.

Now consider Pfizer’s acquisition of Seagen in 2023 for approximately $43 billion. A single biotechnology acquisition commanded a valuation greater than the Philippines’ entire annual BPO revenue at the time. This comparison demonstrates the extraordinary economic value that healthcare innovation can create. Why are we not equally ambitious about building this industry?

The Philippines already trains physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and scientists for healthcare systems around the world. Yet much of this talent is exported individually instead of being organized into domestic enterprises capable of developing intellectual property, technology, and internationally competitive products. We can begin with clinical trials, diagnostics, medical devices, pharmaceutical manufacturing, healthcare software, and specialized research services. Healthcare could become another pillar of economic growth.

In April 2026, the Philippines joined Pax Silica, a US-led initiative focused on strengthening supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and advanced technology. The government is planning a major industrial hub in New Clark City, with medical-related industries identified among its potential activities.

Are our medical associations, universities, hospitals, and healthcare investors developing proposals to participate? Could we attract international medical device manufacturers, diagnostic technology companies, and healthcare AI developers? Healthcare leaders should engage early, working with economic agencies to ensure healthcare becomes a strategic national industry that creates the jobs, investment, exports, and tax revenues needed to sustain healthcare expenditure in the future.

I respect the physicians and civil society organizations demanding stronger PhilHealth financing. Their concerns are justified. But achieving universal healthcare requires a politically feasible transition away from discretionary assistance, greater accountability from healthcare providers, stronger institutions, and an economy capable of sustaining rising costs.

If the BPO industry can generate more than $40 billion annually, why should we continue treating healthcare only as a fiscal burden? Reaching our destination requires political realism, institutional execution, and a much bigger economic vision. Let’s not just argue over the slices. Make the pie bigger. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform. The views expressed are his own.

Jire Carreon/Rappler
Senator Rodante Marcoleta is facing a plunder case due to questions related to his P75-million campaign donations

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan 3rd Division has suspended Senator Rodante Marcoleta from his position due to his pending plunder case, the chamber announced on Monday, October 19.

“In the Sandiganbayan’s Resolution penned by Justice Karl B. Miranda and promulgated today, October 19, 2026, Senator Rodante D. Marcoleta is suspended from his position as Senator of the Republic of the Philippines and from any other public office which he may now or hereafter be holding for a period of 90 days from receipt of this resolution,” the 3rd Division said.
“His suspension shall automatically be lifted upon the expiration of the 90-day period from the implementation of this resolution,” it added.

In July, the Office of the Ombudsman filed the non-bailable case against Marcoleta due to questions related to the P75-million campaign donations to him. Aside from plunder, the senator was also charged with three counts of alleged violation of Presidential Decree No. 46 (receiving gifts).

Section 5 of Republic Act No. 7080 or the Plunder Law declares that any public officer charged with the case “whatever stage of execution and mode of participation, is pending in court, shall be suspended from office.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Burnham pledges ‘big changes’ to the way the welfare system works to tackle Neets crisis – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Prime minister’s comments come as children’s commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza highlights ‘staggering’ inequalities in young people’s treatment across UK

Good morning. Children and young…

blocks.text: Good morning. Children and young people are at the top of the agenda today, with the publication of a hard-hitting report from Dame Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England, and a Times article by Andy Burnham. They are focusing on slightly different cohorts – Burnham is writing about young people who leave school and enter the benefits system, while the de Souza reports covers the experiences of young children in multiple aspects of their lives – but their overall message is the same: the younger generation is being let down.

De Souza has studied more than 160 datasets to examine how what happens to children as they grow up varies across England and she says the variation is “staggering”. In her report, The Childhood Lottery, she explains:

double quotation markIn four local authorities, the total amount spent on youth services per teenager is the princely sum of £0, £421 less than in the highest spending local authority. Some areas of the country are sending nearly 90% of their looked after children to out-of-area placements, compared to the almost 20% in the areas making least use of these – although given this means being away from family ties, and friends, that is still worryingly high. But what stands out is not merely these differences, but how much work there is to do to deliver a happy, healthy childhood in every postcode. I have made the difficult decision to highlight the 20 places where it is hardest to grow up. I want to be clear that this is not a review of the local authority, this is an assessment based on a wide range of measures looking at the challenges faced, the full range of services available and the outcomes we see. We cannot shy away, though, from the fact that poor education outcomes, long health waiting lists or simply feeling unsafe converge in particular places.
The report identifies Middlesbrough as the most challenging place to be a child, and Cheshire East as the least challenging place. I will publish fuller tables shortly.
The overall picture is grim too. Here is an extract from the report’s summary.

double quotation markThe data pulled together in the Childhood Lottery highlights the scale of challenges faced by children across all areas of the country and all areas of their lives. For example that: -Over 1 million children (1,048,965) had active referrals to children and young people’s mental health services in 2024-25.1 -Most pupils (55%) do not achieve a good standard in their English and Maths GCSEs (grade 5 or better in both) at the end of key stage 4. -There are around 1 million young people in the UK aged 16 to 24 not in employment, education or training (NEET) -Approaching half (44%) of looked after children are placed outside their local authority area. Far too many care leavers (40%, plus 6% with unknown activity) are Neets [not in education, employment or training]. -12% of children said they did not feel safe in their local area.

The Burnham article is specifically about Neets. The government was expected to publish Alan Milburn’s final report with recommendations on Neets before the budget. Now it is coming next month, which means the pitch-rolling process ahead of publication is unusually protracted. Milburn has given an interview to the Guardian and, as Anna Bawden and Kiran Stacey report, he is explicit about wanting some benefit payments to be cut to fund more employment support.
In his article, Burnham accepts that many people people today feel “shut out”.

double quotation markThere is no shortage of people lining up to take a swing at the next generation but, if we are honest, the blame for this failure lies with politicians. At the very moment growing up became harder, the support young people relied on was stripped away. Youth services were practically abolished. Children’s mental health services were cut. Families were left to fight for support for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The pandemic stole two years, and social media is too often taking something much deeper: their confidence and sense of belonging. Add an education system focused on the university route and a job market offering too few opportunities, and we should not be surprised that so many are shut out.
And he signals that he is going to follow Milburn’s recommendations on benefits.

double quotation markToday, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, a goodbye. Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job … This will be our offer: a clear guarantee of support. But it will also be matched by an expectation that young people will take up the opportunities made available to them. This will mean big changes to the way our welfare system operates. Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point. The system will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to. It will begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them.
Here is the agenda for the day.
10am: Daisy Cooper, the Lib Dem deputy leader and Treasury spokesperson, holds a press conference on Lib Dem budget proposals.
Morning: Andy Burnham is on a visit in South Wales linked to the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster (which is on Wednesday).
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2.30pm: Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
3pm: Dame Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England, gives a speech at at the launch of her Childhood Lottery report.
After 3.30pm: MPs debate amendments to the Northern Ireland Troubles bill.
5.30pm: Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, gives a speech on devolution.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: West Bank: Israel arrests 10 suspects over settler attacks on US journalist, European diplomats
articles.summary: Israeli police made the arrests following attacks on a US journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank. Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has reported at least 170 settler attacks…

image.caption: The attack on veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine comes after global outrage over mounting settler violence in the West BankImage: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: Israeli police said Monday they had arrested 10 suspects over settler violence in the occupied West Bank, including attacks on a US photojournalist and European diplomats.
Masked settlers were filmed assaulting The Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine on Friday while she was covering a Palestinian olive harvest, leaving her with broken vertebrae.
The following day, settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats and French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was visiting the West Bank to help with the harvest.
The incidents drew condemnation from the United States, France, Belgium and Poland.
Israeli police said the investigation was ongoing, while Israeli media reported that the Shin Bet domestic security service was involved.
European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers
What did the authorities say?

Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's West Bank commander, said "an arrest operation was conducted before dawn" following "the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians."
Foreign Minister ⁠Gideon Saar and the Israeli military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attacks on the diplomats.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination" ⁠with the Israeli military. He added that the facts of the attack on ⁠Levine were "unclear."
The attacks came ahead of the crucial October 27 elections for Netanyahu.
West Bank olive harvest under attack
Will the Israeli settlers face prosecution?
Settler violence against Palestinians has surged, with at least 170 attacks reported since September 27, according to Israeli human rights group Yesh Din.

DW's correspondent in Jerusalem, Tania Kraemer, said Palestinians, journalists and international observers have little confidence that the arrests will lead to charges against the alleged perpetrators.

Citing a study of Israeli police investigations into violence against Palestinians in the West Bank by Yesh Din, Kraemer said only about 3% of investigations between 2005 and 2023 ended in a full or partial conviction.
More than 80% were closed because police failed to identify suspects or gather sufficient evidence, the Yesh Din report said.

articles.title: Deepfakes, bots and distrust: How AI is shaping Israel's election
articles.summary: For the first time, AI is playing a major role in Israel's elections. Observers warn that deepfakes, bots and influence campaigns could sway voters.

image.caption: Netanyahu's Likud has used AI in its campaign more than any other major partyImage: Ohad Zwigenberg/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a 19-second clipposted to X, Gadi Eisenkot, a candidate for prime minister, stands with his arms outstretched and a huge smile on his face. In slow motion, he runs through a meadow toward a person who resembles his son, wearing a shirt with the words "Israeli Unity." But Eisenkot sails past him and instead embraces Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab politician who leads the Ra'am party, running in the elections.

The video was posted on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's account. Opinion pollsshow Netanyahu and Eisenkot, who also happens to be a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, in a tight race. The AI-generated video appears to be designed to play on anti-Arab sentiment — a big part of Netanyahu's campaign.
The clip was viewed more than 1 million times and stirred outrage. Eisenkot's son was killed in 2023 during the Israel-Hamas war.

According to Ze Be AI, a research project of the Open University of Israel, monitoring AI content in the 2026 legislative election campaign, this clip is just one of more than 1,800 posts with AI-generated content that Netanyahu's Likud party had released throughout the election campaign by mid-October. That represents about a quarter of the Likud party social media materials analyzed by Ze Be AI.

blocks.caption: Netanyahu posted this AI-generated clip of rival Gadi Eisenkot on X in July. It was viewed more than 1 million timesImage: x.com/netanyahu

blocks.text: On October 27, Israelis will vote in an election that could oust Netanyahu from power or cement his grip on the country for the coming years. Political scientists are already calling it Israel's first AI election. Parties have been deploying AI across every aspect of campaigning — from creating outrageous videos aimed at stirring controversy to robocalling voters and unleashing bots online.

"There is a scenario where, in a strategic point shortly before the election, AI could or would be used in ways that would steer controversy that could tilt the election results," said Anat Ben-David, a media researcher leading the Ze Be AI project at the Open University of Israel.
AI videos go mainstream

Ben-David and her research team have been tracking all of the content posted on social media by politicians since the end of July. By mid-October, they had collected more than 44,000 posts across Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok and found that over 14% of the material used AI in some way.
A hybrid approach was most common, with AI being deployed for a part or segments of an ad: in images, music, subtitles, logos or full-fledged deepfakes.

Some fringe parties use the greatest ratio of AI in their content. But Likud is the winner by far when it comes to sheer numbers of AI use in content analyzed by the team. Netanyahu's party is followed his left-wing rivals, the Democrats, and then Eisenkot's party, Yashar — though at far lower numbers.
Israel's Central Elections Committee issued a new rule in July mandating that all AI-generated or -manipulated content in election campaigning be labeled. Beyond that, there are few limits.
"There's no AI Act, no Digital Services Act, and the privacy law is very outdated," Ben-David said. "Then you see new [AI] uses that would be impossible to see in Europe."
Some of those uses have come from Israel's most prominent politicians.

Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, has been trying to capitalize on popular internet trends. One videolabeled as AI content features him sitting under a ceiling fan — with each rotation of the blade, his outfit changes: from an army uniform to a T-shirt with the popular slogan "bring them home now" (referring to Israeli hostages in Gaza) to a suit and tie.

In one photorealistic AI video, posted by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich in September, Israel's attorney general and Supreme Court justices are apprehended at an anti-government protest. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara has frequently clashed with the ruling coalition.

blocks.caption: An AI-generated video posted by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich shows Israel’s attorney general and Supreme Court justices being detained at an anti-government protestImage: x.com/bezalelsm

blocks.text: And National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir shared an AI-generated video of Palestinians being wheeled on a conveyor belt into what looks like a concentration camp. That post drew widespread condemnation, with Germany's Foreign Ministry calling it"completely unacceptable" and "abhorrent."
The election authority has shown some willingness to intervene. In July, its chairman ordered Smotrich to take down an unlabeled AI video it called misleading.
A new generation of robocall
It's not just deepfakes and ads: AI is also being used to reach voters directly.

Some voters are getting a new kind of AI-powered robocall — far more conversational than the robotic automated calls of the past. Nitsan Yasur, a disinformation researcher at the Israel InternetAssociation, shared a recording with DW of a four-minute phone call.
Netanyahu's final campaign? — Israel heads to the polls

In it, a voice introduces itself as a pollster named Danielle with an Israeli polling institute and asks for his voting preferences. When Yasur asks if the voice is human, it admits, "there is no human agent on the line," before continuing to ask, "would you like to continue with the short survey?"

The bot fields several of Yasur's questions, while always steering back to who he would vote for. But when Yasur asks five times who commissioned the survey, it doesn't reveal the information. So it remains unclear whether this was part of an election campaign or a poll. What is clear is how advanced robocalling has become.
"You don't need real people making real phone calls, which are obviously limited in time and capacity," Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler, a senior fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, told DW.
Efforts to shape what chatbots tell voters
Some Israelis are also turning to AI for advice on how to vote.
About a quarter of Israelis said they would consider using AI tools or other online services to inform their voting decisions, the Israel Internet Association found in a survey.

That raises concerns about generative engine optimization (GEO): creating online content designed to be picked up by AI chatbots and shape their answers. The Israeli government has already tapped this industry. According to filings under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, it paid a US firm to build websites meant to feed LLM systems with content supportive of the government in order to make AI chatbots more pro-Israel.
"The same industries are going to be used now inwards in order to affect the elections," she said.
Bot accounts promote Netanyahu online

There's fake content, and then there are fake audiences. Scooper, an Israeli company specializing in media monitoring, told DW that it discovered a network of inauthentic accounts boosting Netanyahu on social media. On X, more than 1,000 new accounts have been appearing daily and immediately following the Israeli prime minister. His Instagram following has also surged in recent weeks.

About 70% of the accounts that share Netanyahu's posts on X are based outside of Israel and resemble bots, Scooper research manager Gil Feldman told DW. Feldman said the company flagged them by looking for suspicious behavior such as round-the-clock posting, recent creation dates and missing profile pictures.
Israelis demand accountability for October 7

And it's not just Netanyahu: The Israeli watchdog FakeReporter found a bot campaign linked to Ben-Gvir's campaign, which his office denied. FakeReporter discovered a network of more than 100 accounts, some using AI-generated images and identities, targeting Smotrich and others.

Though bot networks are nothing new, AI can make them cheaper and easier to run. And, because Israelis are early and eager adopters of new technology, Shwartz Altshuler sees the country as a test case for how AI is reshaping elections around the world.
"The whole machinery of political propaganda is becoming totally different," Shwartz Altshuler said.

articles.title: Helen Haines updates: PM says person in custody after alleged attack on Helen Haines; police say she is in critical condition
articles.summary:
Independent MP injured in an incident involving a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria. Follow updates

‘No ongoing threat to community’: Victoria…

blocks.text: Victorian police release statement
Victorian police have released a statement, and said they have arrested a man who allegedly struck a women with a vehicle in Wangaratta.
Police say the woman – known to be Haines – is in hospital with “critical injuries”.
Police allege it was a white Toyota Landcruiser that struck Haines on Murphy Street at about 3.35pm, and that there was a knife seized from inside the vehicle.
The statement says:

double quotation markWhen he exited the Toyota, the driver, a 43-year-old Tarrawingee man, was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident. The woman was taken to hospital with critical injuries. A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota. At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act. It is not known yet if the parties are known to each other. Major Collision Investigation Unit detectives are en route. The investigation remains ongoing.
Key events

items: 10m agoVictorian police release statement
21m agoPM says suspect in custody after alleged attack on Haines
34m agoHelen Haines' family release statement

blocks.text: Acting Superintendent, Ashley Mason, says he was “not aware” of any prior concerns or incidents related to Helen Haines before today’s incident.
Asked how long the area will remain a crime scene, he says:

double quotation markWe’ve got our investigators from the Major Collision Investigation Unit who are currently en route to Wangaratta from Melbourne. So they’ve got significant travel time as well as the time it will take for them to thoroughly process the crime scene once they arrive. I think. There’s some talk that there might be specialist terrorist related police involved in the investigation. We’ve notified our crime and counter–terrorism command and they’re currently liaison and assisting our investigators.
‘No ongoing threat to community’: Victoria police
Mason tells journalists there is “nothing to indicate at this stage” that the two parties are known to each other, but police are still investigating.
He says there is no ongoing or further threat to the community or any other individual at this stage.

articles.title: Independent MP Helen Haines fighting for life after incident outside Wangaratta office in regional Victoria
articles.summary:
PM confirms a man is in custody after the Indi MP was left in a critical condition after being struck by a car on Monday afternoon

The independent MP Helen Haines has been critically injured…

blocks.text: The independent MP Helen Haines has been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, confirmed on Monday night that a suspect was in custody and that the alleged attack on Haines was being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce.
He said the motive for the alleged attack was not known, and would not comment on whether the suspect was known to police.
In a statement, Haines’ family confirmed that she had been injured and thanked bystanders for their assistance.
“This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care,” they said in the statement.
“We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response.
“Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media.
“Please keep Helen in your thoughts.”

In a statement, Victoria police said a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, about 10km from Wangaratta, was in custody and that a knife had allegedly been found in his car. They alleged he had been detained by a passerby when he exited the car.
The statement said the woman that was struck was in a critical condition.
“Police have arrested a man after a woman was struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta this afternoon.
“It is understood a white Toyota LandCruiser struck the 65-year-old woman outside an office on Murphy Street about 3.35pm.
Police said that they were investigating as to whether it was an intentional act, and it was not known if “the parties are known to each other”.
Emergency services had been called to the scene of the incident at Murphy Street on Monday afternoon.
According to the Victorian Emergency Services website, two vehicles responded and the road was closed after the incident.
In a social media post, the Nationals MP, Michael McCormack, said it was “such awful news”.
“Sending my love and best wishes to Helen Haines for a full and speedy recovery,” McCormack said.
Police were expected to release a statement regarding the incident on Monday night.
Haines has represented the electorate of Indi since 2019.

articles.title: Dong Gonzales posts bail for graft raps before Sandiganbayan
articles.summary: Former Pampanga Rep. Aurelio Dong Gonzales has posted bail in the second and seventh divisions of the Sandiganbayan over the graft charges he is facing for alleged ties to government contractor firms…

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 4:19pm

Former Pampanga Rep. Aurelio Dong Gonzales has posted bail in the second and seventh divisions of the Sandiganbayan over the graft charges he is facing for alleged ties to government contractor firms while he was in office.
The respective clerks of court confirmed this for the anti-graft court's divisions. Bail was set at P90,000 per count.
Gonzales posted bail before the Second Division on Friday, October 16, and the Seventh Division last Saturday, October 17.
Another graft case filed by Ombudsman prosecutors vs. Gonzales is pending before the Sandiganbayan Third Division.
In an earlier press conference, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Gonzales’ graft charges violate Section 3 of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, the conflict-of-interest clause.
“This is the usual story where there is a divestment, but it goes back to him. The money goes back to him, so there was really no real divestment,” Remulla said.
“Because if you look at the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records, the payment for construction companies where he supposedly divested still goes to his private bank accounts," he added.
"We have testimonies from engineers and the AMLC has given us financial records on which we based our conclusion,” Remulla said.
Gonzales served as congressman representing the third district of Pampanga from 2007 to 2013, and again from 2016 to 2025. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: No Pinoys arrested or hurt in France unrest — embassy
articles.summary: The Philippine Embassy in France said that no Filipinos had been arrested and no casualties involving Filipino nationals had been reported amid the unrest in the country.

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 4:18pm

Police officers stand behind a fire near Place de la Republique following an unauthorised demonstration, central Paris, on October 18, 2026 a day after nationwide protests against the "high cost of living."
AFP / Matthieu Rondel
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Embassy in France said that no Filipinos had been arrested and no casualties involving Filipino nationals had been reported amid the unrest in the country.

In a statement on Sunday, October 18, the Philippine Embassy in France said that while it noted several violent incidents and cases of property damage in parts of France, including Paris, no casualties or legal detentions involving Filipino nationals had been recorded.

“Pinapayuhan ang mga Pilipino sa France na manatiling kalmado, iwasan ang mga lugar ng protesta at malalaking pagtitipon, at sundin ang mga tagubilin ng mga lokal na awtoridad,” the embassy’s statement read.
(Filipinos in France are advised to remain calm, avoid protest sites and large gatherings, and follow the instructions of local authorities.)
The embassy also reminded the Filipino community to maintain strict political neutrality, refrain from participating in local political disputes, and exercise restraint.

Filipinos residing in or visiting France were advised to follow all directives from local police, monitor official announcements regarding road closures and public transport disruptions, and ensure that family members were kept informed of their whereabouts.

The embassy also reminded the public to exercise caution on social media, verify information before sharing, and refrain from spreading unverified reports or inflammatory comments that could cause unnecessary panic.
Filipino nationals requiring urgent consular assistance may contact the Philippine Embassy in Paris through its dedicated hotlines and official channels:

items: Assistance-to-Nationals (ATN) Hotline: +33 6 80 11 52 71
Consular hotline: +33 6 20 59 25 15
Email: [email protected]

blocks.text: France has been experiencing civil unrest since September, with protests over the cost of living, fuel prices, and deteriorating public services.

The movement began as a month-long student protest over teacher shortages and poor school conditions, then broadened into anger over inflation, fuel prices, inequality, public spending cuts, and declining public services.
Trade unions, students, and groups linked to the “yellow vest” movement joined the mobilization.
On October 17, about 550,000 people marched nationwide, including 110,000 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry, while organizers put the turnout at more than 800,000.

articles.title: Bangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia said it executed two Bangladeshis last week for committing an "indecent act" in a mosque.

blocks.text: Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.

A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.

According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.

The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.

Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A resolution urging the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) to recommend declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata was filed at the Senate on Monday. Sen. Erwin…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A resolution urging the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) to recommend declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata was filed at the Senate on Monday.
Sen. Erwin Tulfo filed Senate Resolution No. 739 following Jing’s statement that China “may easily win” if it wanted to use force in a confrontation over the West Philippine Sea.

The resolution sought to “urge the Department of Foreign Affairs to recommend to the appropriate authorities the declaration of Ambassador Jing Quan as persona non grata, in view of the severity of his remarks and their implications for Philippine sovereignty, national dignity, and bilateral relations.”
It also sought to “express [the Senate’s] serious concern over the remarks made by the Ambassador China to the Philippines Jing Quan suggesting the potential use of force against the Philippines.”
Since Oct. 16, a day after Jing made the statement in an interview, some lawmakers have expressed the need to declare him persona non grata in separate statements.
In response, the Chinese Embassy urged the declaration through its social media pages, saying it should be made or lawmakers should “stop bluffing.”
The embassy pressed further on Sunday, characterizing the persona non grata declaration as “old and low tricks.”
“If they really want to do something, do it quickly and immediately, please,” the embassy added.
It also claimed that “anti-China politicians” who spoke about declaring Jing persona non grata “will not [be] welcome” to China. /mcm

articles.title: Marcos does not want Chinese ambassador expelled, says Palace
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has not signaled any intent to declare China’s ambassador persona non grata, the Palace said on Monday, October 19, though the Chinese diplomat today has been…

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 4:10pm

Secretary of Foreign Affairs Ma. Theresa Lazaro on Oct. 19, 2026 summons Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan to convey the Philippines’ serious concern and strong objection to his public statement of October 15, which conveyed a threat of the use of force.
Department of Foreign Affairs via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has not signaled any intent to declare China’s ambassador persona non grata, the Palace said on Monday, October 19, though the Chinese diplomat today has been officially summoned by the Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We know the president’s view. He would not want this kind of declaration, against any representative of another country here in our country,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro told reporters in Filipino at a briefing. She was asked about calls from senators and congressmen to expel Ambassador Jing Quan.

On the same day, Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro formally summoned Jing and told him his October 15 remarks, said at a chance interview, were “provocative and unacceptable,” the DFA said in a statement.

The department also rebuked the Chinese embassy for its public attacks on lawmakers. It was “not the place of a foreign mission to publicly criticize or taunt Philippine officials and legislators who are acting within their mandates,” the DFA said. It reserved the right to take further diplomatic action, but did not say what that could involve or how Jing responded.
Castro said the Palace respected the views of lawmakers seeking Jing’s expulsion, but that Marcos would not go down this road as of yet.
“Everything he says can affect our country and our people,” she said.
The DFA has previously described declaring a diplomat persona non grata as an “option of last resort” that carries heavy diplomatic consequences.

JUST IN: Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro summons Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan to formally object to remarks he made last week, which the DFA says conveyed a threat of the use of force against the Philippines. @philstarnews https://t.co/QXpMwqYpwM — Cristina Chi (@chicristina_) October 19, 2026
‘We may easily win’

Jing made the remarks in question to reporters on the sidelines of a forum in Quezon City last week. Denying that China was a troublemaker, he said the Philippines should feel fortunate to have China as a neighbor. “If we want to use force, we may easily win,” he said, adding that China would not do so because it loves peace.
That evening, the DFA said the diplomat's words would seem to convey a “thinly veiled threat of the use of force."
Marcos reacted on October 16 and said the remark “sounds very much to me like a threat” and that he wanted to understand what the ambassador meant.

The embassy accused the DFA of selectively quoting and overinterpreting the ambassador. As senators called for Jing’s expulsion, the embassy dared them on Facebook: “Is this threat or coercion? But anyway, just do it. Otherwise, STOP BLUFFING.”
Sen. Erwin Tulfo earlier said the Senate majority plans to file a resolution seeking to have Jing declared persona non grata.

articles.title: Business owner faces up to 20 years in prison over Canada waste importation
articles.summary: A Manila court has sentenced a business owner to up to 20 years in prison for illegally importing hazardous waste materials from Canada, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said.

This file photo shows one of the 69 containers of waste that were returned to Canada from the Philippines at Global Container Terminals after being offloaded from the Anna Maersk container ship, in Delta, south of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada June 29, 2019. Darryl Dyck/Pool via REUTERS
A Manila court has sentenced a business owner to up to 20 years in prison for illegally importing hazardous waste materials from Canada, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said.

In a statement, the DOJ said the Manila Regional Trial Court (RTC) found the business owner guilty of aiding and facilitating the importation of hazardous waste in 10 container vans at the Port of Manila in June 2013.
The court sentenced him to 12 years and one day to 20 years in prison and imposed a P1-million fine, with subsidiary imprisonment in case of insolvency.
According to the DOJ, the shipment was initially declared as compressed plastic scrap.

However, it contained mixed, unsorted and heterogeneous plastic materials that allegedly entered the country without the required clearance from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR).

articles.title: Senate reso urges declaration of Chinese envoy Jing Quan as persona non grata
articles.summary: Senator Erwin Tulfo on Monday filed a resolution calling on the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) to recommend declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, following his contentious…

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 4:04pm

Senator Erwin Tulfo on Monday filed a resolution calling on the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) to recommend declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, following his contentious statement that Beijing could “easily win” if it resorts to force against the Philippines.

Under proposed Senate Resolution No. 739, Tulfo, vice chairperson of the Senate committee on foreign relations, said that Jing’s remark “raised serious concerns over the propriety of diplomatic conduct and its implications for Philippine sovereignty and national security.”
The senator said the diplomatic relations between the Philippines and China “must be anchored on mutual respect, constructive engagement, and peaceful dialogue.”

He urged the DFA to recommend to the appropriate authorities the declaration of Jing as persona non grata, in view of the severity of his statements and their possible effects for the country’s sovereignty, national dignity, and bilateral relations with China.

To recall, a social media post by Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea, Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, showed Jing being interviewed, where he said, "If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not use force. You know, we love peace, and in this region, we enjoy the peace."

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. said he would summon the Chinese Ambassador following his remarks, which the chief executive said “sounds very much like a threat,” and is “not a very diplomatic statement to be made.”
On Monday, the DFA formally summoned Jing to convey the Philippine's "serious concern and strong objection" to his recent remarks.
The Chinese Embassy earlier released a statement asking if the statement of some lawmakers declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata was a “threat or coercion.”
"But anyway, just do it. Otherwise, STOP BLUFFING," the Chinese Embassy added. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: West Philippine Sea: Teodoro reiterates PH troops not troublemakers
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Monday maintained that Philippine troops in the West Philippine Sea were defending the country’s rights under the United Nations…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Monday maintained that Philippine troops in the West Philippine Sea were defending the country’s rights under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) and were not seeking to provoke trouble.

“Consistent with our earlier pronouncements, number one, we refute all allegations made by the ambassador that we are troublemakers and are provoking. We reiterate, Your Honor, our support and promotion of the Unclos and the UN (United Nations) Charter,” Teodoro said during the Senate finance subcommittee hearing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of National Defense (DND).

Teodoro’s remarks came following the Department of Foreign Affairs’ (DFA) move to summon Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan on Monday to formally protest his Oct. 15 remarks about the use of force perceived by Philippine government officials as a threat meant to intimidate the country.
Teodoro was sought for comment on how the DND treats such a public statement by the Chinese official.

“Secondly, we have already indicated our objection to his speech, because he not only said once, ‘You lose’. What is being portrayed now is, ‘We can use force if we want, but we may win easily’,” he added, quoting Jing. “There was also another thing he said, ‘Okay, you cut military communications, but you lose’. So that means there’s a threat there. And he said that twice.”

Teodoro stressed that the Philippines’ objection was clear, not just to the Chinese ambassador’s statement, “but more importantly, their false narrative with the nine-dash line, that they have jurisdiction.”

“Third, their latest narrative that Batanes is part of China, saying they now have the right to operate in the waters surrounding Batanes. That is strongly opposed, and we are trying to deter that kind of behavior,” he added.

Now that Jing has already been summoned by the DFA, Teodoro said they will have to wait for developments, adding that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. or the DFA will message the public about the issue at an appropriate time. /dl

articles.title: Bank fraud victims want Ottawa to make big banks pay more
articles.summary: Every year, Canadians lose hundreds of millions to bank fraud — and are often left footing the bill. Now, customers of TD, Royal Bank, Scotiabank, CIBC and the Bank of Montreal are calling on Ottawa…

image.caption: Dozens of bank fraud victims, some who've lost their life savings, ask why banks aren't held more liable for losses. (CBC)

blocks.text: Over 10 months, Ralph Moore lost $450,000 to an online investment scam — drawn in, in May 2025, by a deepfake video of Prime Minister Mark Carney, heralding a new government investment platform where people could safely grow their savings.
The 88-year-old did transactions online and made multiple trips to his local TD Bank to arrange transfers, bank drafts and payments to other people's credit cards.
Now, Moore and his family are asking why the bank didn't do more to stop the transactions — and won't reimburse him.
"I don't think they protected me," he told Go Public from his home in Qualicum Beach, B.C.
His daughter Leslie Herrndorf, who lives in another city, says she was incredulous when she learned what happened.

items: Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

blocks.text: "How could $450,000 be allowed to be given away by a bank who'd been dealing with my dad for decades?" she asked. "They knew this was unusual behaviour."
Shortly after discovering the bank fraud, Herrndorf had her father's mental capacity tested. He failed.
When Ralph Moore tallied up the money he'd withdrawn from TD Bank, it totalled more than $450,000. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

Early on, the bank recognized that Moore was falling victim to a scam. It took some steps — questioning several of Moore's transactions and warning him and his wife about scams. It also alerted its fraud and anti-scam teams and at one point placed temporary restrictions on his account.

But Herrndorf wonders why the transactions weren't permanently blocked, her father's account frozen, or why the bank didn't make an effort to reach out to its client's adult children or possibly contact the police.

They are among the more than three dozen victims of bank fraud contacted by Go Public for this story who want to know: why doesn't Ottawa hold banks more liable for fraud, like some other countries do?
"It is outrageous, with the known number of frauds happening, that a bank has decided that this is the level of customer service that's acceptable," said Herrndorf.
Moore's daughter Leslie Herrndorf only learned her father was the victim of bank fraud when it was too late. Her father, a longtime TD Bank customer, had lost $450,000. (Michael McArthur/CBC)

Bank fraud is a massive and growing problem, according to the government's Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. It reports people lost more than $700 million to all fraud in 2025 — and estimates only five per cent of victims report when it happens. Banking-specific numbers were not available.
Go Public receives emails almost daily from people who've suffered fraud losses: from e-transfer fraud to the bank impersonator scam to investment scams and credit card fraud.

items: TD Bank holds customer responsible for $15K loss, won't say how account hacking ruled out
New tuition scam left woman with $37K in fraudulent charges — and no help from bank, police or school
RBC and CIBC allow 89-year-old to drain life savings, lose $1.7M to scammers

blocks.text: In almost all cases, financial institutions hold their customers accountable – issuing similarly worded denial letters, in which people are accused of sharing passwords and account information or blamed for co-operating with scammers posing as investment experts, bank employees or other authorities.

"These are not negligent people, not stupid people," said Alexandre Plourde, a lawyer and analyst at Option consommateurs, a Montreal consumer advocacy organization that also regularly hears from bank fraud victims.
"I don't think the law does enough to protect consumers."
Go Public requested interviews with TD, Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank and CIBC after submitting inquiries about various customer losses at all five banks. All declined.

items: See statements from the big five banks

blocks.text: In February 2026, after Moore had lost virtually all of his money, TD shut down his account.
In a letter to Herrndorf written July 31, 2026, TD said it decided to "exit the client relationship" to "prevent further financial harm."

In a written statement to Go Public, a TD spokesperson did not answer any questions about Moore's case, citing client confidentiality. He said that protecting customers "remains a top priority through robust security, monitoring and education resources" and encouraged victims of fraud and scams to file reports with authorities.
'Zero responsibility'

Scotiabank customer Karla Zwicker says hackers stole over $13,000 from her accounts and line of credit last year. The bank said there was no evidence her account was compromised and declined to reimburse her.
"They've got to stop blaming the customers," said Zwicker, of Edmonton. "We need the government to do more."

Ivanka Bubic believed she was co-operating with RBC's fraud department last year, when scammers spoofed the bank's phone number and convinced her to withdraw money from her line of credit and approve charges on her credit card.
Moore was misled by a video like this that he saw online – a deepfake of Prime Minister Mark Carney, encouraging Canadians to invest in an online platform. (Michael McArthur/CBC)
RBC reimbursed its Montreal customer about $26,000 in credit card charges, but said she was responsible for $15,000 taken from her line of credit.
"It's crazy that they have zero responsibility when fraud happens," she said.

Deepak Kadaba of Mississauga, Ont., lost $3,400 to unauthorized withdrawals and debit transactions. BMO said the withdrawals were completed using his banking information, and the bank is therefore not liable.
"They're hanging customers out to dry," said Kadaba. "Where are the protections?"
'Big incentive' for Canadian banks
Cases like this often have very different outcomes in the U.K.
Since October 2024, the U.K. makes financial institutions shoulder the responsibility for fraud losses, except in cases of extreme negligence.
"The bank must reimburse consumers when they're a victim of fraud … unless the consumer has been grossly negligent," said Plourde, the lawyer. "That's a very high threshold for the banks to prove."
He says Moore's $450,000 loss is "unacceptable" and when customers are clearly being scammed, banks "should have protocols to go deeper, ask more questions."
Go Public requested interviews with TD, Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank and CIBC after submitting inquiries about various customer losses at all five banks. All declined. (CBC)
Other jurisdictions, like the E.U. and Australia, have also introduced laws that can force banks to reimburse fraud victims in many cases — though none have gone as far as the U.K.
"Putting more liability on Canadian banks would be a big incentive for banks to develop better security measures," said Plourde.

The Canadian Bankers Association, a trade group, told Go Public that "placing further liability on financial institutions alone will not prevent scams" and could "unintentionally have a negative impact" on bank customers and the economy.
Calls for liability laws
Consumer advocates like Plourde, some MPs and the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments have called on Ottawa to make the banks pay for fraud losses for several years.
But when the federal government introduced changes to the Bank Act on March 26, 2026, there was nothing about holding the banks responsible.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne recently told CBC News that he takes bank fraud seriously, and outlined several new measures the government is taking, including working on a national anti-fraud strategy.
"We're acting. We're not waiting, we're acting," said Champagne.
He did not commit to holding financial institutions accountable for fraud.

items: Rogers cutting telco customer service jobs amid complaints of long wait times
TD Bank holds customer responsible for $15K loss, won't say how account hacking ruled out
This Calgary woman won a $13K settlement — but says her paralegal kept the money

blocks.text: Meanwhile, a new survey released Oct. 13 by Option consommateurs found that Canadians overwhelmingly (87 per cent) believe that banks should reimburse victims of banking fraud, except when the customer has been grossly negligent.
The survey was conducted by Léger earlier this month, and involved just over 1,500 Canadians.
"The survey results show a public consensus on the need to strengthen banks' obligations," said Plourde.
"We're reaching record highs of fraud every year," he added. "It's time to act."

Banking on Fear: CBC Marketplace continues this investigation, seeing first-hand in the U.K. how British banks are now incentivized to stop fraud before it happens. Watch as the team confronts a scammer: Friday, Oct. 23 at 8 p.m. ET on CBC Television (8:30 p.m. NT) or stream anytime on CBC Gem and the official CBC Marketplace YouTube Channel
Submit your story ideas
Go Public is an investigative news segment on CBC-TV, radio and the web.
We tell your stories, shed light on wrongdoing and hold the powers that be accountable.

If you have a story in the public interest, or if you're an insider with information, contact gopublic@cbc.ca with your name, contact information and a brief summary. All emails are confidential until you decide to Go Public.

articles.title: NATO's race against time: Senior commander warns alliance must adapt faster to deter Russia
articles.summary: NATO's supreme commander of transformation says the West's greatest vulnerability may not be a shortage of weapons, but the time it takes to build them — and the speed at which its adversaries are…

image.caption: NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Transformation Pierre Vandier says in a contest with Russia, the West’s greatest vulnerability may not be a shortage of weapons. It may be time. He spoke to CBC News recently during a trip to Ottawa. (Murray Brewster/CBC)

blocks.text: There's a nightmare that keeps one of NATO's most senior military commanders up at night and it's not what you might think.
It isn't the idea of Russian tanks rolling into the Baltic states or Poland. Nor is it a sudden military confrontation in the Arctic.

The scenario that keeps NATO Supreme Allied Commander Transformation Pierre Vandier up at night is the notion of the Western military alliance being caught unprepared and unable to keep up with the pace of technological innovation that's happening on the modern battlefield.
"Being late is really my nightmare," Vandier, a French admiral, told CBC News in an exclusive interview.

items: In Canada's drone-killing 'Sandbox,' companies compete for a $1M prize

blocks.text: "When I see people chatting, delaying some important decisions, not committing the money, using some … old-fashioned process, then it keeps me [up] at night."

Vandier met Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan and other high-ranking defence leaders for an up-close look at some of Canada's defence innovation plans during his recent low-key trip to Ottawa.
His warning about keeping pace comes at a particularly uncomfortable moment for the 32-member alliance.
'Being late is really my nightmare,' says NATO commander

Russia's war against Ukraine is approaching its fifth anniversary. Moscow has been accused of escalating a campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions in Europe along NATO's eastern flank. And Western governments are scrambling to rebuild military capabilities and defence industrial production lines that were allowed to shrink following the end of the Cold War more than three decades ago.
The danger, according to Vandier, is that the alliance is trying to prepare for tomorrow's war using institutions, procurement systems and assumptions inherited from yesterday.
"We thought that time was our friend," he said. "Now time is not our friend. It's the enemy's friend. The agenda is built on the other side."

During four years of grinding combat in Ukraine, Russia has suffered an enormous number of casualties. According to the British Ministry of Defence, as of mid-September, the Russian military has suffered 1.3 million casualties in the Ukraine war, including over 500,000 dead.

And there is a paradox at the heart of NATO's current security dilemma. While there have been devastating casualties and an enormous amount of equipment lost, the Russian Army that stumbled into Ukraine four years ago is not the same one on the battlefield today.
Vandier argued that Moscow has become more innovative, more adaptable and, in certain areas, more dangerous.
"The enemy is not the same as the one we had in 2022," he said.
"They learn, they adapt."
How NATO is flexing in the face of Russian aggression
He pointed specifically to Russia's evolving drone technology, including faster jet-powered attack drones that have complicated Ukraine's ability to defend its cities and critical infrastructure.
According to Vandier, the introduction of more advanced propulsion systems has significantly reduced the effectiveness of some Ukrainian drone-interception methods.

He estimated that interception success rates against certain Russian drones have fallen from approximately 90 per cent earlier this year to roughly 50 per cent as the technology has evolved. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, at the end of September, pegged the interception rate at about 55 per cent.

There's been a significant body of research published over the past year which challenges the assumption that Russia's enormous losses in Ukraine have left its military weaker, less capable or unable to threaten NATO.

Western military analysts increasingly describe a Russian military that has learned to adapt under fire, regenerate formations while fighting, absorb technological innovation and sustain operations despite staggering casualties.

items: How NATO is prepping in the Baltic skies for a possible confrontation with Russia
Putin appears to be eyeing NATO. The question is, will he actually attack?

blocks.text: "Russian military institutions reward loyalty over competence," said a study written last July by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, which argued Russia has become increasingly dependent on Chinese, Iranian and North Korean military assistance.
The authors argue that Russia's military can absorb new technology without developing the capacity to exploit it fully and effectively.

An assessment written last year by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), based in the United Kingdom, was even more stark. It pointed to how Moscow is rebuilding equipment inventories, expanding units and reorganizing forces near NATO territory.
The think-tank's report said that Russia may restore important elements of its prewar ground-force equipment strength sooner than expected, although newly formed units could remain undermanned.

The IISS report also suggested that equipment shortages throughout the Russian military could potentially be resolved by late 2026 or early 2027. However, the full equipping and expansion of Russian ground forces could take until 2030 or 2035.
"It's a very fast-evolving environment," Vandier said.
Why 'grey zone' drone attacks are a problem for NATO

Russia has the ability to produce enormous quantities of relatively inexpensive drones and missiles. And that has exposed the limitations of Western defence industries designed to manufacture smaller numbers of highly sophisticated weapons.
Vandier believes the alliance has underestimated the scale of the challenge.
"The idea that the war is just a crisis of a few weeks is something that nobody can bet on anymore," he said.
He pointed to the enormous numbers of drones and missiles being employed in Ukraine as evidence that NATO must rethink not only what it buys, but how quickly it can replenish its arsenals.
The problem, Vandier said, is not simply a shortage of weapons. It is a shortage of industrial capacity.

Western economies have spent decades moving manufacturing and critical supply chains overseas, leaving defence industries dependent on materials and components that may not be readily available during a prolonged conflict.

items: Why Russia has Europe on edge
Norway PM 'prepared, but not afraid' of Russian incursion

blocks.text: Vandier challenged the suggestion that NATO's combined economic strength automatically translates into an overwhelming industrial advantage over Russia.
"I disagree with the point where we have a good industrial depth," he said.
"The challenge now is to produce what we can produce in mass and rapidly, and not only what we have on a very exquisite and limited quantities."
The implication of that is significant. In a prolonged conflict with Russia, the West would quickly run out of equipment and ammunition.
The U.S-Israeli war with Iran has seen a number of published reports about the scarcity of high-end weapons systems.
For Canada, Vandier's assessment comes as the federal government embarks on an unprecedented expansion of defence spending.
After decades of relatively limited investment, Ottawa has committed billions of additional dollars to modernizing the Canadian Armed Forces and rebuilding the country's defence industrial base.
Vandier said he has been struck by the scale of the change.
"It's very impressive to see how this country, which has spent a limited amount of money focused on NORAD, now is opening eyes on all the NATO [area of responsibility]," Vandier said.

articles.title: DPWH eyes November award of key Bataan-Cavite bridge section
articles.summary: The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) aims to award a 3.1-kilometer section of the Bataan-Cavite Interlink Bridge (BCIB) by next month, subject to approval of the Asian Development Bank…
articles.byline: JON VIKTOR D. CABUENAS, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 3:50pm

The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) aims to award a 3.1-kilometer section of the Bataan-Cavite Interlink Bridge (BCIB) by next month, subject to approval of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), which is co-financing the project.

Based on the BCIB’s Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) uploaded on the DPWH website, the section set to be awarded next month is Package 6 of the BCIB, which involves the South Channel Bridges and Approaches.

“Mag-a-award kami ng (We will award the) P6, which is the most critical part of Bataan-Cavite, within November. It’s already pending with the ADB for concurrence,” DPWH Secretary Vivencio “Vince” Dizon told reporters on the sidelines of the EJAP Infrastructure Forum in Makati City.

Package 6, or the South Channel Bridge, will be located between Corregidor Island and Cavite, the bigger of the two proposed cable-stayed bridges. It will have a span of 1,800 meters between the two pylons, creating an opening for ships to pass through as they go in and out of Manila Bay.

It will also feature two monopole-style towers standing 346 meters above the seabed, or about 306 meters above sea level. It will likewise have a “Nearshore Navigation Channel” provided near the Cavite shoreline.
“‘Yung foundation kasi nung P6, ‘yung matataas na tore. Ang dalawang foundation na ‘yan na malalaki, igugulong. Each foundation is bigger than Araneta Coliseum, just as a trivia,” Dizon said.
(The foundation for P6 are the tall towers. The two massive foundations will be rolled out. Each foundation is bigger than the Araneta Coliseum, just as a trivia.)
The BCIB is planned as a 32-kilometer bridge connecting Mariveles in Bataan and Naic in Cavite, expected to cut travel time between the provinces from five and a half hours to 45 minutes.

The project is bankrolled through a multi-tranche financing scheme, under which the Asian Development Bank (ADB) will finance $ 2.1 billion, while the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) will co-finance $1.14 billion. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos prefers diplomacy over declaring Chinese envoy persona non grata
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. does not want to declare any foreign diplomat persona non grata, including Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan, as the country remains…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. does not want to declare any foreign diplomat persona non grata, including Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan, as the country remains keen on resolving issues through diplomatic means, Palace press officer Claire Castro said Monday.

This comes as the Senate is eyeing a resolution on the Chinese embassy’s challenge to Filipino lawmakers to declare Jing persona non grata over his remarks about China’s use of force against the Philippines.

Earlier this year, Castro warned that declaring Chinese diplomatic personnel persona non grata carries serious implications and should be considered only as a last resort when diplomatic relations have severely deteriorated.
Asked whether Malacañang still stood by that position, Castro said Marcos would not want to declare any foreign official in the country persona non grata.
“We know the president’s position. He would not want this kind of declaration to be made against anyone, including a representative of another country here in our country,” she said at a briefing.

“Whatever the opinions of other leaders and senators may be, we respect their views, opinions and feelings. But as we have said, the president does not act outside diplomatic channels,” she continued.
Castro added that Marcos continues to regard relations between the Philippines and China as “good” despite a war of words between the Chinese embassy and Philippine officials.

“Relations remain in good standing in the eyes of the President and the administration. If there are issues like this, let us allow the Department of Foreign Affairs to respond and determine the appropriate steps to further improve dialogue with China,” she said.

Castro said there was no information yet on when Marcos would summon Jing. However, the president would proceed with his scheduled trip to Shenzhen, China, from Nov. 18 to 20 for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting.
She also said there was no information on whether Marcos and Chinese President Xi Jinping would hold a bilateral meeting.
Castro maintained that the Philippines would not initiate aggression in defending its interests in the West Philippine Sea.
“Even as we fight for and protect our rights, our territory and the West Philippine Sea, the President remains diplomatic. He does not initiate any aggression,” she said.
“That is what we should show and make known to the whole world: that the Philippines does not initiate any aggression,” the Palace official added.
She said the government remained hopeful that relations with China would improve.
Meanwhile, Castro said lawmakers and other officials would not be prevented from expressing their concerns about the issue, as they enjoy freedom of expression.
Last week, Marcos said he would summon Jing over the envoy’s remarks that China could easily win if it chose to use force against the Philippines.
The remarks prompted lawmakers to urge Marcos to declare Jing persona non grata. /das
