articles.title: [EDITORIAL] Cruelty is not wit — itigil ang disabled-shaming
articles.summary: Lalo pang nanuot sa buto ang kababawan, kayabangan, at 'feeling superior' na attitude laban sa may kapansanan dahil sa mindless vanity culture ng Instagram at Facebook

blocks.text: Lalo pang nanuot sa buto ang kababawan, kayabangan, at 'feeling superior' na attitude laban sa may kapansanan dahil sa mindless vanity culture ng Instagram at Facebook

Nakauuga ang pangungutya ng Machong Chismisan kay Josh Aquino, anak ni Kris Aquino na nasa autism spectrum. Nakauuga rin ito dahil muling masisilip dito ang maitim na budhi ng Philippine media culture.

blocks.caption: animated, josh Aquino, matching chismosa,autism

blocks.text: Nagagalit tayo, hindi dahil anak siya ni Kris Aquino — but inspite of it. Imagine, kung ang anak ng prestihiyosong pamilya’y hindi nakaligtas maging fodder sa sick jokes ng mga insecure male scum — paano na ang mahihirap na neurodivergent?

Disability should never be a punchline. ‘Yan ang reaksiyon ng Autism Society of the Philippines. At lalo nang hindi dapat maging cheap punchline for a room full of laughing men. (Basahin dito kung interesado kayo sa buong kuwento ng disabled-bashing.)

To use the impeachment trial’s favorite word last week, “binangga” ng toxic masculinity ang persons with disability movement. Siyempre, ililibing nang buhay ang fake macho hosts ng Machong Chismisan. Pero hindi puwedeng back to normal programming pagkatapos nito. Kailangang may magbago.

Hindi lang ito dapat maging race to say what’s politically correct. Dapat maging salamin ito sa lipunang Pilipino na tawang-tawang manlait ng mahihina at may kapansanan. Ilan ba sa mga nagmamalinis ang secretly ay kiliting-kiliti kapag sinusundot ang mga hindi pasado sa depenisyon ng lipunan ng “normal” at “maganda”?
Hindi dahil nagkalat na ang mga asosasyong tulad ng Autism Society at naipasa na ang mga batas laban sa diskriminasyon ay masasabing humupa na ang masamang ugaling ito.

If anything, lalo pang nanuot sa buto natin ang kababawan, kayabangan, at “feeling superior” dahil sa mindless vanity culture ng Instagram at Facebook. Sa social media, wala sa hulog ang pangit, mahina, at higit sa lahat, hindi “normal.”

Matagal nang ingrained sa kultura natin ang ganitong mentality dahil sa impluwensiya ng noon-time shows na nag-go-glorify sa mga lalaking nagpapamalas ng casual cruelty sa mga babae, sa may kapintasan o may kapansanan.
Sa kaso ng Machong Chismisan, barako banter, edgy comedy, at irreverent wit kuno ang excuse nila para manlait at manlibak ng kapwa.

Tila bigo ang lipunan nating magturo ng empathy mula sa duyan. Hindi lang tolerance ang kailangan ng mga disabled at neurodivergent. Kailangan nilang mapangalagaan, at ma-integrate bilang productive members ng komunidad.

Araw-araw, humaharap ang mga pamilyang nagpapalaki ng anak na may Down syndrome, autism, at iba pang disabilities hindi lang sa backward attitudes, kundi pati sa systemic hurdles. Struggle sa kanila ang humanap ng tamang paaralang affordable pero inclusive, at lalo na affordable health care. Pagkatapos igapang sa pag-aaaral, walang puwang ang mga disabled na kabataan sa workforce na biased sa manggagawang may developmental disability.

On the cultural front, we have to force Philippine media to grow up. Kailangan ng bystander intervention sa harap ng ganitong cruelty, online and offline. Huwag palusutin ang disability-shaming. Huwag i-click, huwag i-patronize ang cavemen antics ng mga sangganong naglipana ngayon online.
Hindi caricature si Josh — ayon sa mga kaibigan at pamilya niya, siya ay malumanay, mabait, at madasalin. Inaalagaan niya ang nanay niyang may sakit.

Sabi ni Senadora Risa Hontiveros, chair ng Senate committee on women, children, family relations and gender equality: “The true measure of our character is how we treat the most vulnerable members of our society.”
Hindi ito dapat magtapos sa apologies. Whole of society effort ang inclusivity, at dapat maganap ito sa antas ng komunidad, paaralan, batas, at higit sa lahat, sa social services ng pamahalaan.
Dahil ang press release natin, disenteng tao tayo. Fake it till we make it. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Teachers’ group says looser uniform rules won’t fix classroom heat during strong El Niño
articles.summary: A teachers’ group has urged the Department of Education to shorten class hours when necessary, adopt hybrid learning arrangements and invest in classroom cooling amid the looming El Niño.

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 1:10pm

MANILA, Philippines — A teachers’ group has urged the Department of Education to shorten class hours when necessary, adopt hybrid learning arrangements and invest in classroom cooling amid the looming El Niño.
The group said relaxed uniform rules alone will not protect students and teachers from extreme heat as a strong El Niño sets in.

In a statement Monday, October 19, the Teachers’ Dignity Coalition (TDC) said it recognized Education Secretary Sonny Angara’s acknowledgment that adjustments, including letting students wear a sando, may be needed.

The group said schools should wait for a formal DepEd policy on official uniforms for both learners and teachers. It warned that unclear rules could cause confusion among schools and add costs for families.
“The issue must not be reduced to what learners and teachers are allowed to wear,” the group said.

Angara announced on Friday, October 16, that public school students would no longer be required to wear uniforms, citing the anticipated heat inside classrooms during El Niño. He told reporters students could come to class in a sando or other informal clothing, provided it was reasonably dignified.

The state weather bureau PAGASA has put the odds of a “very strong” El Niño at 81%. It expects the event to develop between October 2026 and January 2027, with a 97% chance that El Niño conditions last through the first half of 2027.

Department of Science and Technology Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. has said every province could face drought or very dry conditions by the end of March 2027. More than 100 municipalities have already declared a state of emergency ahead of the phenomenon.
The Philippines last went through very strong El Niño events in 1982-1983 and 1997-1998.
El Niño during the school year

This looming El Niño will take place during the current school year. Under a transition plan set in 2024, classes for School Year 2026-2027 were to run from mid-June 2026 to March 2027, restoring the old calendar that keeps students out of school during the traditionally hottest months of April and May.
PAGASA, however, projects the El Niño to peak in October, November and December.
In April 2024, extreme heat forced more than 4,000 schools to suspend in-person classes, affecting over 2.4 million students, according to DepEd figures at the time.
Beyond uniforms, TDC asked DepEd to consider shorter instructional hours and hybrid arrangements that combine face-to-face classes with other learning modes.

However, it also cautioned: "These arrangements should not result in a wholesale shift to purely modular or online learning, which may disadvantage learners who lack reliable internet access, digital devices, or suitable learning spaces at home."

Over the longer term, the group called on the government to invest in clean and renewable energy for a steadier electricity supply. It also asked for better classroom ventilation, cooling systems, and air-conditioning where feasible.
“The fundamental concern is whether our schools can provide safe, healthy, and conducive learning environments despite the effects of climate change and extreme weather conditions,” TDC said.
Angara has said DepEd is studying the installation of more solar panels in public schools so classrooms stay cooler and students can keep learning even in intense heat.

At the Senate hearing on his department’s budget, responding to Sen. Bam Aquino’s questions on school preparedness, he said students should be sent home once temperatures hit 40 degrees Celsius, or even sooner, because they risk headaches and nosebleeds.

In July, DepEd opened nationwide consultations on a proposed executive order that would automatically suspend in-person classes and onsite work when hazard thresholds are met, including a heat index of at least 40 degrees Celsius.

articles.title: Erwin Tulfo 'hurt' by 3 senators' vote backing ouster petition
articles.summary: Sen. Erwin Tulfo on Monday said he was hurt by the reported vote of three fellow senators in favor of a petition seeking to unseat him.

blocks.text: Sen. Erwin Tulfo on Monday said he was hurt by the reported vote of three fellow senators in favor of a petition seeking to unseat him.

This came after the Senate Electoral Tribunal (SET) denied a motion for reconsideration seeking to reverse its earlier dismissal of a quo warranto petition seeking to unseat Tulfo over alleged citizenship issues, among other grounds.
The motion was denied with six SET members voting in favor and three against.

“Alam mo, ipapasa-Diyos ko na lang ‘yan. Medyo nasaktan lang ho ako dahil dalawa po doon sa tatlo—’yung isa talagang ganoon na ho talaga ang ugali, wala naman tayong magagawa, medyo may sama ng loob yata sa akin—pero ‘yung dalawa, lalo na ho ‘yung isa, niyayakap ko pa, nagkakamayan pa ho kami… halos magkadikit ho ang opisina namin,” Tulfo said in an interview on Super Radyo dzBB.

(You know, I’ll just leave it to God. I was a bit hurt because of the three, I already know what one of them is like, and there’s nothing we can do about it. That person may have some ill feelings toward me. But the other two—especially one of them—we still embrace and shake hands. Our offices are practically next to each other.)
Tulfo also hinted that one of the senators involved was a woman who had been his colleague in the House of Representatives.
“’Yung babae naman ho, ‘yung isa pa naman eh kasamahan ko dati sa Kongreso, pagkatapos po eh nag-uusap naman ho kami eh,” he said.
(As for the woman, she was a former colleague of mine in Congress, and we still talked to each other.)

“Dati may issue ho siya. Noong medyo may problema, binati ko ho, ’di niya ako binati. Pero after one week, pinansin niya ho, sabi niya, ‘Sorry ha, sir, dami lang running from my mind.’ Sabi ko, ‘It’s okay, Sen, no problem.’ Sabi niya, ‘Basta we’re friends.’ Sabi ko, ‘Sure.’ Kaya nagulat ako sa balita,” he added.

(There was an issue involving her before. When she was having problems, I greeted her, but she did not respond. A week later, she spoke to me and apologized, saying she had a lot on her mind. I told her it was okay. She assured me that we were friends, and I agreed. That’s why I was surprised by the news.)

Over the weekend, Tulfo, a neophyte senator, posted a cartoon on his official Facebook page depicting three individuals preparing to stab him in the back. The arms holding the knives bore the names “Sen. Padilla,” “Sen. Villar” and “Sen. Pia.”
A speech bubble above the three arms read, “Alisin yan sa Senado!!” (Remove him from the Senate!)

The SET is composed of three Supreme Court justices and six senators. Senators Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan, Bam Aquino and Lito Lapid represent the majority bloc, while Senators Pia Cayetano, Robin Padilla and Camille Villar represent the minority.
Tulfo, however, said he could not confirm the identities of the three SET members who allegedly opposed him, adding that the voting details were supposed to remain confidential.

“Tatlong Supreme Court associate justice ang bumoto na ibasura at tatlong majority. Silang tatlo daw, hindi. Pero hindi ko ma-confirm ’yun dahil confidential ’yan eh. Pero ’yun ho ang lumalabas ngayon,” he said.

(Three Supreme Court associate justices voted to dismiss the motion, along with three senators from the majority bloc. The three senators reportedly said they did not vote against me. But I cannot confirm that because the information is confidential. Still, that is what is coming out now.)
“Eh kung ganoon nga ho ’yan na sila nga, eh medyo nasaktan tayo. Kaya ipapasa-Diyos ko na lang ho ’yan, may karma naman ho eh,” he added.
(If they really were the ones involved, then I would be hurt. So I’ll just leave it to God. There is such a thing as karma, after all.)
GMA News Online has reached out to the offices of Padilla, Villar and Cayetano and will update this story once they issue a response.
On Saturday, Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson also questioned the motives behind the votes of three SET members who reportedly belonged to the minority bloc.

“Justice and fairness went out of the window when three minority senator-members voted in favor of an out-of-time motion for reconsideration filed by a petitioner without legal standing. Their motive may be deeper than personal issues against Sen. Tulfo,” Lacson said in a post on X.

The quo warranto petition against Tulfo was filed by Berteni Cataluña Causing, who cited the senator’s alleged American citizenship, disloyalty to the Philippines and allegiance to the United States, membership in a political dynasty, and lack of academic qualifications as grounds for his disqualification.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists
articles.summary:
Voters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold second binding independence vote

Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum…

blocks.text: Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum that has exposed deep divisions within the province, not least in the separatist movement itself.
On Monday, voters will respond to the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada, or hold a second binding independence referendum.

A minority have long argued that separation is the only way to address their belief that Alberta is short-changed by its financial relationship with Ottawa, and prevented from fully exploiting the province’s vast fossil fuel reserves.

Any enthusiasm either side might have held headed into the referendum was muted after a deadly fire broke out at a major military base in the province. On Saturday afternoon, a blaze tore through the CFB Wainwright and into the nearby town. Canada’s armed forces announced with “profound sadness” that there had been multiple deaths and injuries.
The premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, argued for years that a referendum was not needed, but called one anyway after pressure from some within her United Conservative party.

blocks.caption: Alberta’s premier, Danielle Smith, called a referendum after pressure from some within her United Conservative party. Photograph: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP

blocks.text: Nevertheless, Smith did not campaign in favour of independence, saying in June she estimated the cost of separating at about C$400bn (£212bn) for the transition and another $25bn-$50bn in annual costs associated with starting a new country. Smith’s caution prompted some of her supporters to accuse her of betraying the independence movement.

Opponents of independence have focused heavily on the costs of separation, with the University of Calgary’s school of public policy saying in June it could be up to $170bn over a five-year period and be highly unpredictable in the long term.

The issue has not divided neatly along partisan lines. The former premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley – from the rightwing Conservative and leftwing New Democratic party – have appeared on stage together, setting aside a bitter ideological rivalry that more usually defines Albertan politics.
Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” the prime minister told a raucous crowd.
Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, saw first-hand the effects of the Brexit vote and the economic upheaval that followed.

“This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said. “Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

blocks.caption: Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada. Photograph: Megan Albu/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Carney, whom recent polls identify as the most popular politician in Alberta, joined the former deputy premier of Alberta Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for the latter’s Forever Canadian group. Lukaszuk has driven more than 40,000km (24,855 miles) around Alberta in a 1992 motorhome named the Unity Bus and distributed at least 100,000 lawn signs.

Rather than campaigning frequently, Carney has pointed to big projects his government is looking to move ahead with that would benefit the province, including a pipeline to the Pacific coast to increase the flow of Alberta crude oil to Asia.
“I won’t sugar-coat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” said Carney.

Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa, stemming from the 1980 national energy programme, which sought greater federal control over the energy sector, provoked fierce opposition in Alberta and helped erode Liberal support across western Canada. The sense that the province’s wealth was being siphoned eastward is older still: a 1915 cartoon, “The Milch Cow”, depicted Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as farmers feeding a cow whose milk was funnelled into buckets labelled Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal.

“Growing up, I remember. I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” Carney told the crowd. “And more recently, we were made to feel that our energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

blocks.caption: Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa. Photograph: Jeff McIntosh/AP

blocks.text: The movement seeking to capitalise on those grievances, however, has been marked by competing interests, personal rivalries and allegations surrounding some of its leading figures. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is alleged to have mismanaged millions of dollars of First Nations trust funds, while David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organiser, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.

Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of the province’s modern separatist movement, recently published the Alberta transition plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning it into an independent country.

Rejecting comparisons to Brexit and the economic fallout, Wilson said: “Every single thing we found that needs to be addressed to do the transition is absolutely doable,” calling most of the tasks “super easy”.
Wilson dismissed the idea that negotiations between an independent Alberta and Canada’s federal government would be acrimonious and lengthy.

“It would be economic suicide for them to challenge Alberta,” he said. “You want to cut off trade with us? OK. By the way, go buy axes and chainsaws because you’re going to have to cut down all the maple trees to keep warm this winter because you’re not going to get our energy products.”

Even within the separatist camp, there are doubts about how quickly independence could be achieved. Bill Jones, a member of the Wildrose Independence party, said its leaders were moving too quickly without the institutions a new country would need, from a police force to a pension system.
“We – Alberta – were always meant to be a colony, to get resources that were here to go east,” said Jones. “And that mindset is still there.”
“I don’t see the evidence for our independence. If we go out today, we’d be a failed state for generations. The great-great-grandchildren would be still suffering. And that’s the problem.”
Monday’s referendum will also include nine other measures unrelated to separation, including proposals affecting social programmes, judicial appointments and the senate.

One remain campaign has distributed thousands of “no to the nine” lawn signs around the province. Even some separatists, angry at Smith, have started a “decline the 9” campaign. Smith, for her part, has pushed a “yes to the rest” message in response.
In Calgary, the city’s mayor said he was “duty bound” to speak out about the perils of an attempt to fracture the country.

“There will be catastrophic impacts that would arise from separation,” said Jeromy Farkas. “And the unfortunate bullshit implication of separation is that it’s invited a conversation about who is a ‘real Canadian’? Who is a ‘real Albertan’? If you are living here in Calgary, you are welcome here. We need to continue to signal that. We need to telegraph that stability.
“We stand to lose so much from simply even having this debate.”

In October, further details emerged about meetings between unelected Alberta separatists and both Republican operatives and staff at the US state department. Among items allegedly discussed were how oil royalties could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country. They also allegedly offered up Alberta’s fresh water resources.

No matter the results on Monday, the referendum could have looked far different if not for the intervention of First Nations, which successfully sued to force the Alberta government to either dismiss the question of separation or change the wording. Key to their argument was the fact that the land of modern-day Alberta is covered by five treaties signed with the crown before the creation of the province.

blocks.caption: Protesters highlight concerns about Indigenous treaty rights and the broader implications of Alberta’s separation. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

blocks.text: The president of the Blackfoot Confederacy, Chief Troy “Bossman” Knowlton, said: “These treaties are living documents, but the ignorance of the separatists, and their bigotry, does not allow their mind to accept the fact that they’re not symbolic documents. They have power, and the reality is Alberta does not have the constitutional right to separate.”

Knowlton said that if separatists had proactively reached out to First Nations before pushing ahead with independence, it might have led to a different outcome. “But they treated us as a speed bump they could just drive over.”

He added that the First Nations’ legal victory was followed by what he viewed as recriminations from the province, including an unexplained halt to talks on land claims and cooperation with Alberta’s government.

“At the end of the day, we want Alberta to continue to be a beacon of light,” he said. “Because when the first newcomers came to these lands centuries ago, that’s what our chiefs said: we’ll share these resources we have here. So do we want prosperity for Alberta? You’d better believe it.”

articles.title: Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian town as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals
articles.summary:
Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the fastest-warming places in the world

Residents of a remote town in Norway that…

blocks.text: Residents of a remote town in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.

Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.

blocks.caption: In the fastest-warming town on the planet you can’t drink the tap water. Here’s why – video

blocks.text: Longyearbyen, 800 miles from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate, with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4C a decade.

Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost – rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer – and the geology of the former mining town.

“The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard.

blocks.caption: Marjolaine Verret takes water samples. Photograph: Tonje Emilie Stenstad/The Guardian

blocks.text: When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidised and generated acidity, she explained. “The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks.”

The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per litre recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year. The mayor of Longyearbyen, Terje Aunevik, said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic”.
Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants.

Emergency, temporary measures were rolled out, including the installation of a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery, for residents to refill containers at the local supermarket, and an investigation was launched.
Manganese levels have since dropped, but earlier this year sulphate and nickel levels were found to exceed recommended drinking water limits. As a result, the ban remains in place.

Aunevik said that while manganese levels were “not dangerous”, government guidelines had to be followed. The drinking water crisis had created a lot of “noise”, he admitted, with some residents angry at the inconvenience.

blocks.caption: The exposure of bedrock by thawing permafrost has leached metals into the Isdammen lake, the source of Longyearbyen’s water. Photograph: Tonje Emilie Stenstad/The Guardian

blocks.text: The mayor, who has commissioned an investigation into water quality, said a “completely new water mains supply” may be needed. Potential solutions being considered were installing a filtration system to Isdammen and having a desalination plant as a backup, or the other way around. Either way was “extremely expensive” and, due to the extreme temperatures of Svalbard, with water temperatures often below zero, would include technical challenges, Aunevik said.

“In Norway, where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it is challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water like we do now. Other small communities should be precautious and start thinking of what to do if it happens to their sources.”
Verret and other scientists have warned that the contamination of water sources in Longyearbyen could be a foretaste of what is to come for Arctic communities.

“These ingredients [bedrock rich in pyrite and heavy metals] and thawing permafrost are present in other parts of the Arctic so this could be a first example of how climate change can impact freshwater, for example in northern Canada and Alaska,” Verret said.

articles.title: Burnham urged to launch inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution
articles.summary:
Letter from 150 scientists, MPs and activists calls for action to protect lower-income and minority-ethnic communities

The government must hold an inquiry into the unequal impacts of air…

blocks.text: The government must hold an inquiry into the unequal impacts of air pollution, 150 scientists, MPs and activists have urged.
Research by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows that across England, lower-income areas have persistently higher levels of air pollution than wealthier areas.
The same research found that minority-ethnic populations were exposed to air pollution levels that were about 6% higher than those experienced by white populations.

In a letter signed by 150 scientists, MPs and activists, including the climate activist Greta Thunberg, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been urged to hold a national inquiry into the impacts of air pollution on these groups.

Exposure to air pollution is linked to heart disease, strokes, cancer, asthma and effects on lung development in children. Despite this, the letter says, the UK does not have a dedicated mechanism to address the health inequalities.

Air pollution can come from a wide range of sources, from wood-burning stoves to industrial fossil fuel burning. But the leading threat to clean air is posed by traffic emissions, with petrol and diesel vehicles emitting a variety of toxic pollutants. Measures such as London’s ultra-low emission zone have had a significant impact on improving air quality, with children’s lungs found to have grown bigger and stronger as a result of the policy.

While there has been marked progress in reducing air pollution in cities like London, new government data shows that in 2025, parts of London, Glasgow and Bristol still had illegal levels of air pollution.

Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, the mother of a nine-year-old girl who became the first person in the UK to have air pollution cited on their death certificate, said a “failure of inaction by all the main political parties over so many years, has meant the UK population is exposed to illegal levels of emissions”.

This warning comes as new data, obtained through freedom of information requests by the campaign group Mums for Lungs, shows that in 11 English cities and areas, including London, Greater Manchester and Birmingham, more than 200,000 children were taken to hospital with breathing difficulties in 2025. The research found that younger children were the most affected, with more than 120,000 babies and toddlers admitted to A&E or hospital.
Children are particularly vulnerable to air pollution because their lungs are still developing and they breathe more air relative to their body size than adults.
In the city of Manchester, there has been a stark increase in admissions of babies and toddlers, rising from 653 in 2023 to 1,072 in 2025.
after newsletter promotion

Mums for Lungs said the decision in 2023 by Burnham, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, to scrap plans for a clean air zone raised important questions about whether sufficient action was being taken to drive down pollution levels.
Jemima Hartshorn, the campaign group’s founder, declared the situation an “air pollution emergency”.
“Behind every number is a child who is struggling to breathe and a family looking for help. We cannot keep treating dirty air as inevitable or acceptable,” she said.

A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “Air quality continues to improve over the longer term and while most air quality standards are being met, more action is needed to protect communities.

“Our ambitious new targets will cut harmful particle exposure by nearly a third by 2030. Working together with local authorities will keep driving progress through clean air plans and robust monitoring.”

articles.title: Up to 20 maternity units in England may have to shut, NHS leader warns
articles.summary: Exclusive: NHS Alliance’s acute care director says centralisation of services ‘inevitable’ to ensure safe care

blocks.text: Up to 20 maternity units in England will have to shut to ensure mothers and babies receive safe care amid shortages of doctors and rising caesarean section rates, an NHS leader has warned.

Matthew Hopkins, the NHS Alliance’s director for acute care, said centralising childbirth services into fewer hospitals was “inevitable” and the “right thing”, but would lead to a political backlash against unpopular changes.
Ministers must “grasp the nettle” that as many as 20 of England’s 155 NHS units that are led by consultant obstetricians will need to shut or change their role, he added.

Hopkins urged ministers and MPs to show “courage” by backing major changes to where maternity services are located, even though reconfigurations will lead to mothers-to-be in affected areas being forced to travel further to have their babies.

Smaller maternity units that deliver only 1,500 to 2,000 babies a year are becoming increasingly unsustainable because of a widespread lack of obstetricians and a sharp rise in recent years in the number of women having either a planned or emergency caesarean section, he added.

Many of the units most at risk are in rural or coastal areas, where staffing is particularly challenging, he told the Guardian. “We are calling for a thorough appraisal of maternity services and where they need to be located because the current configuration is not fit for purpose,” Hopkins said.
“Difficult decisions lie ahead, consolidating maternity services to support safer, more sustainable care.
“If politicians … are keen to see safe maternity services in their area, it is going to need courage to grasp the nettle that needs to be grasped in order to improve maternity services.”

Consolidation of care at fewer sites was “inevitable” and represented “doing the right thing … the safe thing for patients”, he said. Maternity units with too few doctors could not provide the level of service needed to ensure safety, he stressed.

Hospital bosses fear that the government’s maternity taskforce, which is due to publish a report on improving childbirth care before Christmas, “will be tokenistic and won’t deal with the real strategic issues that underpin the problems” if it does not set out clearly how the NHS should accommodate the rise in caesarean sections, which require units to have more staff and more operating theatres, Hopkins added.

blocks.caption: Matthew Hopkins said changes were needed to ensure the safety of mothers and their babies. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: But his comments provoked an immediate outcry, with obstetricians and midwives insisting that maternity care should remain a service the NHS provides near people’s homes. “Women and families rely on local maternity units to be there when they need them, and we must ensure there are high-quality services close to home,” said Hannah Leonard, the chief policy officer of the Royal College of Midwives.

Dr Alison Wright, the president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, said: “There are other solutions to our workforce challenges that are far safer than closing maternity units, and these should be explored.”

Hopkins’s comments came as the Royal Devon university healthcare NHS foundation trust was expected to decide this week if the maternity unit at North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple, which shut temporarily in August due to understaffing, now has enough doctors to allow it to safely reopen.

Andy Burnham, in his first appearance at prime minister’s questions on 2 September, admitted that maternity services across the whole UK were facing “structural issues”. Burnham told the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, it was “not acceptable” for expectant mothers from north Devon to have to give birth in Exeter, which is 43 miles – and a 70-minute car journey – from Barnstaple.
An estimated 194 women have had their child in Exeter because of the closure.

The maternity unit at Yeovil hospital in Somerset reopened earlier this year after being shut for almost 12 months because it had too few staff. The maternity unit at Daisy Hill hospital in Newry, in Northern Ireland, was last month earmarked for closure for the same reason. Strenuous efforts by NHS bosses to recruit obstetricians from Ireland, the UK and internationally to work there failed.

Closing rural and coastal units would put mothers and babies in danger, said Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrat health spokesperson. “Forcing women in labour to travel an hour or more to the nearest hospital is unsafe, unacceptable, and leaves local communities abandoned,” she said, adding that ministers must not allow maternity services in rural and coastal areas to be “shuttered”.
Hopkins – who has run four hospital trusts – is not the first senior figure to argue for major reconfiguration of maternity services to improve the quality and safety of care.

Marian Knight, a professor of maternal and child population health at the University of Oxford, who investigates maternal deaths as part of the MBRRACE-UK research programme, told the Health Service Journal last month that the NHS should consider “consolidation into fewer, bigger [maternity] units to help medical teams manage the surge in C-sections”. They rose from 33% of births in England in 2020 to 45% last year.

Some women who died during childbirth between 2022 and 2024 did so because their caesarean section was delayed or postponed because an obstetric surgeon or operating theatre was not available, the most recent MBRRACE-UK report found. “It was not clear if the safety of services is maintained in light of [the] increased demand [for caesarean sections]”, it said.

Urging immediate action on centralisation of care, Hopkins added: “If this C-section rate becomes 55% or 65%, [that] inevitably will force reactive actions being taken. In our view, [and] Marian’s view, we need to grasp the nettle and get ahead of what could be really difficult conditions for mums, babies and staff if this rate of increase in C-sections continues to rise.”

In her government-commissioned review of maternity care in June, Valerie Amos revealed that senior figures in the field had told her that key challenges to improving care included “poor infrastructure, with, at times, unsafe and unacceptable estates … and too little (political) backing for difficult reconfiguration decisions.”
The Department of Health and Social Care was approached for comment.

articles.title: Amelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of trees
articles.summary:
Expedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited island

A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope…

blocks.text: A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solving the mystery of what happened to pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart has said an object they suspected to be her plane was a clump of washed-up trees.

“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University, standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on the atoll of Nikumaroro, about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.

Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished in 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, leading to one of the largest air and sea searches in history. Nearly 90 years later, people are still looking, with Nikumaroro in the archipelago country of Kiribati emerging as a leading candidate for where they might have crash-landed.

Previous visits to the uninhabited atoll have found signs of a castaway camp, a 1930s-era woman’s shoe and other tantalising evidence attributed to the celebrity aviator, including glass from a cosmetics freckle cream jar.
The latest mission stemmed from 2020 satellite images showing an elongated, white object lying in the shallows of the island, near a sandy outcrop called the Taraia Peninsula.

Other longtime Earhart explorers quickly identified it as a fallen tree, but Richard Pettigrew, who heads the nonprofit Archaeological Legacy Institute, found other images, including aerial video showing what he suspected to be a metallic glint in the water.

After a multi-day voyage by ship and subsequent delays due to bad weather, the 17-person expedition managed to pass through the coral-encircled atoll and set up tents to conduct four days of research, including metal detecting. The crew was forced to sleep offshore, partly due to massive land-dwelling coconut crabs, known as “robber crabs” for their inquisitiveness when searching for food.
By Monday, Purdue University confirmed in a statement that the “visual anomaly” was “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit”.

It said the glint was part of a natural process. “The fragment’s reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer. Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand.”

The trip was partially sponsored by the university in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and mentored young female pilots, and which helped fund her modified Lockheed Electra 10-E, known as her “flying laboratory”.

“While we know this is disappointing to many, including us, this mission adds a new chapter in the quest to find the ultimate answer to the mystery of what happened to Earhart during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe nearly nine decades ago,” the university statement said.

The trip adds to a growing list of dismissed hypotheses, including that Earhart – who was the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight – was captured by Japanese forces or that she survived and lived under an alias.

articles.title: [Rear View] Rose Nono Lin’s Lexus and Duterte-era impunity
articles.summary: Pharmally was not an aberration. It was the purest expression of a pandemic response grounded on impunity, indifference, and greed.

blocks.text: In November 2021, at the height of the Senate Blue Ribbon Committee’s inquiry into the Pharmally scandal, Rose Nono Lin was asked about a 2019 Lexus registered in her name, a vehicle worth some P8.8 million. Her answer has since exemplified brazen display of unexplained wealth: “Natagpuan ko po ’yan sa garahe po namin.” She simply found it in her garage.

Lin was corporate treasurer and incorporator of Pharmally Biological, the firm investigators described as the parent of Pharmally Pharmaceutical Corp., which cornered billions of pesos in government contracts for face masks, face shields, personal protective equipment and test kits at the height of the pandemic. Her husband, Lin Weixiong, was Pharmally Pharmaceutical’s financial manager and a close associate of Michael Yang, the former economic adviser of then-president Rodrigo Duterte. Then-senator Richard Gordon, the blue ribbon chair, tagged Yang as the firm’s financier and guarantor. Citing corporate records, the senator called Lin a dummy for her husband, a charge she denied.

Lin had already filed her candidacy for Congress in the fifth district of Quezon City by the time the Lexus issue surfaced. She resigned from Lakas-CMD party, which revoked her nomination. She then snubbed hearing after hearing, until the Senate cited her in contempt and ordered her arrest. The district’s voters turned her down in May 2022. She ran again in 2025, and lost again.

That is the face Pharmally presented to the public. But the scandal was never merely a story of bureaucratic incompetence. It was the story of a scheme that looked at a crisis and saw profit, that saw a market in the sick and the dying.

Pharmally was a company with a paid-up capital of P625,000, an amount that would barely buy a sedan, much less a Lexus. Yet it bagged some P11.5 billion in contracts, the single biggest chunk of the government’s emergency pandemic procurement.

Senators found its supplies overpriced, some of them substandard, and its test kits bought at roughly double what private suppliers were offering. When asked, then health secretary Francisco Duque III pointed to the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) as the procuring agency. The DBM pointed back at the Department of Health’s purchase requests. In short, nagturuan ang DOH at DBM.

On October 16, Ombudsman Jesus Remulla announced the filing of an P11-billion plunder complaint against 46 respondents over the anomalous procurement of pandemic supplies. The list includes Pharmally’s officers, Lin and her husband, Yang, and former head of the DBM procurement service Lloyd Christopher Lao. Thirteen of them, the Ombudsman said, can no longer be located.
It is worth remembering why this took five years.

The Senate committee’s report recommending plunder charges never reached the floor. Duterte’s Senate allies and fence-sitters did not sign the report. It died with the 18th Congress. Remulla’s predecessor, Samuel Martires, filed graft charges, not plunder, saying there was no evidence any official had amassed ill-gotten wealth. Lao was eventually haled to the Sandiganbayan for graft.
Pharmally was not an aberration. It was the purest expression of a pandemic response grounded on impunity, indifference, and greed.

There was money, plenty of it. Money that should have protected families, health workers, and other medical frontliners but went to dubious business entities like Pharmally. Money that should have shored up a public health system on the verge of collapse, or extended temporary relief for qualified beneficiaries. The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) left P780.71 million in “ayuda” unused, depriving at least 139,300 qualified families. Government kept pouring billions into roads and bridges, as if infrastructure could lead us out of a pandemic. What it did not find was the urgency and the focus to get help to people who needed it, despite a state of emergency that was supposed to cut red tape.

Most governments treated the pandemic as a public health crisis. The Duterte administration treated it as a public order problem. We got checkpoints, curfews, combat-ready police and scientifically dubious rules enforced with the zeal of martial law. Quarantine violators were herded into cramped jail cells, and in one Laguna barangay, dog cages. Winston Ragos, a former soldier, was shot dead at a Quezon City checkpoint. The pandemic did not slow down the administration’s drug war and red-tagging. Drug-related killings persisted, and in March 2021, police raids in Calabarzon left nine activists dead in a single day.

We earned the distinction of having one of the longest lockdowns in the world with little to show for it. While our neighbors reopened and recovered ahead of us, we were still told to wear face shields.

blocks.caption: [Ask the Tax Whiz] The Pharmally case: Breaking down tax and financial missteps

blocks.text: And while the public was preoccupied with survival, the powerful saw room to maneuver. House allies revived Charter change. Congress railroaded the approval of the anti-terror law after Duterte certified it as urgent. These political projects proceeded from the same logic of Pharmally’s operators: that people too afraid of the virus and too worried about their next meal would be too exhausted to be angry.
Whether the prize was money or power, there were those in and around government who regarded the pandemic not as a crisis to be managed but as an opportunity to be exploited.

Millions of Filipinos went hungry during those years. Many lost jobs, businesses, and loved ones. Health workers died without adequate protection. And for five years, a Lexus sat in a garage, a monument to Duterte-era impunity.

The Ombudsman’s complaint is a beginning, nothing more. Whether it prospers or dies another quiet death will tell us whether accountability in this country is real or merely performative. Thirteen respondents can no longer be found. The others should be on an immigration lookout list by now. And the rest of us should never forget the Lexus in the garage. – Rappler.com
Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

articles.title: ‘Ti, ano kung Benitez ka?’: Bacolod allies nearly come to blows over city’s debts
articles.summary: A dispute over the city government's debts erupted into a shouting match, with both Bacolod Representative Albee Benitez and a city councilor taking turns in slamming the table as other officials and…

blocks.text: Allies Bacolod Representative Albee Benitez (left) and Councilor Homer Bais (right)
photos from Benitez and Bais social media pages

A dispute over the city government's debts erupted into a shouting match, with both Bacolod Representative Albee Benitez and a city councilor taking turns in slamming the table as other officials and guests looked on

items: A heated confrontation occurred between Bacolod City Representative Albee Benitez and Councilor Homer Bais over the city's P6.1 billion in loans during a MassKara Festival dinner party.
The dispute arose after Bais called for an accounting of the city's loans during a City Council session, leading to a public shouting match that highlighted tensions over financial accountability.
Councilor Wilson Gamboa supported Bais's call for transparency regarding projects funded by loans from both the Leonardia and Benitez administrations, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive audit.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – Bacolod City Representative Albee Benitez walked straight to the table where his political ally, Councilor Homer Bais, was seated at a dinner party. Moments later, a dispute over the city government’s debts erupted into a shouting match, with both men taking turns in slamming the table as officials and guests looked on.
The confrontation threatened to turn physical, prompting Bacolod Councilor Caesar Distrito to intervene. He wrapped his arms around Bais and tried to calm him down.
The commotion eventually subsided, and the two men left the dining area.
The incident unfolded on Friday, October 16, at a MassKara Festival dinner party in the lobby of Bacolod’s New Government Center, during the city’s Electric MassKara parade.
At the center of the confrontation was the city’s P6.1 billion in loans incurred under the past two administrations, including Benitez’s tenure as mayor from 2022 to 2025.
Bais said Benitez confronted him over a manifestation he made during a regular City Council session on Wednesday, October 14, calling for an accounting of the city’s loans.
As Bais tried to explain his position, Benitez slammed the table, he said.
“Albee slammed the table first. I just responded [by doing] the same thing,” Bais told Rappler in an interview on Saturday, October 17.
“Ti, ano kung Benitez ka? (So, what if you are a Benitez?)” Bais shouted.

The retort became a talking point across Bacolod and on social media, where commenters praised the councilor for standing his ground against Benitez, a billionaire politician with considerable influence in the city.
Bais said he was stunned by the confrontation, particularly because it happened in front of fellow officials and guests. He said he had not expected Benitez to confront him that way in public.
The two men are political allies, but the scene they made underscored tensions over the city’s debt and the demand for accountability in the use of public funds.

“May dignidad pa man ko nga dapat tipigan (I still have my dignity to protect),” said Bais, a former anchorman of Bombo Radyo-Bacolod. “I will not and will never allow him to humiliate me in public because I was raised to always stand or fight for what is right.”
Benitez has yet to comment despite requests for comment via SMS and Viber.

Bais said the incident stemmed from a manifestation he made during a City Council session on a proposed resolution by Councilor Em Ang seeking status reports on the unfinished Bacolod MassKara Coliseum and museum-auditorium in barangays Tangub and Alijis.

Ang sought updates on construction, the causes of delays and completion timelines for the projects, which began under former mayor Evelio “Bing” Leonardia and were funded partly by the city’s P1.7 billion in loans.

In the interest of fairness and transparency, Bais said he asked, “Why not include all the projects also funded by other loans of the city?” That proposal would extend scrutiny to projects financed by loans obtained under the Benitez administration.

Councilor Wilson Gamboa Jr., who supported Bais’ manifestation, said the proposal was not ill-intentioned and aligned with Ang’s resolution, which focused on fairness, transparency, financial soundness and accountability.
In July, Gamboa proposed a resolution asking the Commission on Audit (COA) to conduct a comprehensive audit of city projects funded by loans obtained under the Leonardia and Benitez administrations.
The city government secured P1.7 billion in loans under Leonardia, while Benitez obtained P4.4 billion in loans from the Development Bank of the Philippines in 2023, Gamboa said.
The following projects were funded by loans obtained under Leonardia:

items: Construction of the P800-million, 12,000-seat Bacolod MassKara Coliseum and museum-auditorium (ongoing).
Development of the P350-million Progreso Village relocation site (completed)
Site development, construction of a new activity center and facility upgrades at Bacolod City College (completed)
Construction of P200 million worth of roads and bridges (completed)

blocks.text: A document from the DBP Bacolod branch listed the following projects under the Benitez administration’s P4.4 billion in loans:

items: Acquisition of land for various development projects, P2 billion
Construction of a legislative building, P515 million
Construction of mini-hospitals in five barangays, P135 million
Rehabilitation and improvement of the old city hall, P233 million
Rehabilitation and improvement of public markets, P525 million
Improvement and construction of various roads, P300 million
Improvement and construction of various drainage systems, P320 million
Asphalt overlay of various roads, P50 million
Construction of a Bacolod warehouse, P67.9 million
Construction of City Engineering Department motor pool, P30.8 million
Improvement of the tree park in Barangay Alangilan, P47 million
Construction of a pedestrian mall, P50 million
Construction of a city health complex, P220 million
Construction of a recovery and recycling complex and eco-park, P103 million
Construction of a central archives facility, P184 million
Installation of underground cabling, P300 million
Construction and installation of solar power generation systems in various barangays and at the Bacolod City Government Center, P100 million
Construction of traffic signalization systems, P25 million

blocks.text: Gamboa said the city government set aside P560 million in next year’s budget for loan payments, covering both principal and interest.

“It means the city will be paying P46 million per month just for loans,” Gamboa said. “So, it is but natural that we will ask COA’s help to trace all the listed projects funded by our loans.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
articles.summary: Political tension grips France after rioting marred protests over the cost of living and struggling public services, Katya Adler writes.

blocks.text: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history.

On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared.

An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.

There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished.
Macron's speech has been roundly criticised on social media forums and by political opponents for lacking concrete detail.
How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account?
How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time?
Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated?
And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education?

On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France.

He's apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Yet he and his interior minister are charged by many in France with being woefully ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests.
The president of France's lower house of parliament, Yaël Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened this weekend and why.
"Things are dark in the city of light [a nickname for Paris]" was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night.

Macron is widely viewed here as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out. There's a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines.
That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets.
Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks.

Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets.
What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment.
People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation.

Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility.
"While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me.

Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order, posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented".
For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday.

But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests.
France is holding its breath.

articles.title: 'Champi' maintains strength, may regain super typhoon strength before entering PAR
articles.summary: Typhoon Champi may regain super typhoon strength as it approaches the country's monitoring area, with tropical cyclone wind signals potentially reaching No. 3 or 4 over parts of Luzon.

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 12:16pm
Satellite rendering shows Typhoon Champi taken as of 10:00 a.m. of Oct. 19, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Typhoon Champi has maintained its strength while moving west-northwestward over the sea west of Guam and may regain super typhoon status before entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR), PAGASA said Monday.
In its 11 a.m. bulletin on Monday, October 19, the state weather bureau said Champi was carrying maximum sustained winds of 175 kilometers per hour near the center, with gusts of up to 215 kph.
The tropical cyclone is moving west-northwestward at 20 kph, with strong to typhoon-force winds extending up to 720 kilometers from its center.
Champi was last spotted 1,600 kilometers east of Southeastern Luzon, outside PAR.
It is expected to enter the country's monitoring area by Tuesday morning or early afternoon. Once inside PAR, it will be given the domestic name Rosal.
Strong winds, rainfall
PAGASA said tropical cyclone wind signals may be raised over the northern and eastern portions of Northern Luzon and parts of the Bicol Region as early as Monday evening or Tuesday morning.
The highest wind signal in the current forecast scenario is Signal No. 3 or 4.
Gusty conditions may affect most parts of Luzon and the Visayas, as well as portions of Mindanao, beginning Wednesday.
The tropical cyclone is also expected to bring heavy rainfall to Extreme Northern Luzon. PAGASA said a weather advisory will be issued for the affected areas.
Sea conditions
Moderate to rough seas may begin affecting the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon and the eastern seaboards of the Visayas and Mindanao by Tuesday.
Hazardous sea conditions, with very rough to very high seas, may affect the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon from Wednesday onward.
PAGASA said a gale warning for very rough seas is expected to be issued on Tuesday evening or Wednesday morning.
Track, intensity
Champi is expected to continue moving west-northwestward before entering the PAR on Tuesday, after which it will move toward Taiwan while remaining over the Philippine Sea.
PAGASA said Champi may re-intensify beginning Monday evening and regain super typhoon status, with further intensification possible as it moves over the Philippine Sea.
A gradual weakening trend is expected to begin on Wednesday after the tropical cyclone reaches its peak intensity.

articles.title: After the IPO party, GCash comes for 5-6 lending next
articles.summary: 'There’s money in serving them,' says Mynt president and CEO Martha Sazon, as she and her team try to convince investors that lending to underserved Filipinos could fuel GCash’s next wave of growth

blocks.text: 'There’s money in serving them,' says Mynt president and CEO Martha Sazon, as she and her team try to convince investors that lending to underserved Filipinos could fuel GCash’s next wave of growth

items: GCash, with 41.5 million monthly active users, aims to expand its lending services, targeting the informal lending market, which is a significant source of potential borrowers.

Lending currently accounts for 35.8% of Mynt's adjusted revenue, and the company plans to allocate 60% of its IPO proceeds to enhance its loan portfolio, despite facing risks associated with non-performing loans (NPLs).
Mynt's IPO has generated strong demand, valuing the company at approximately P442 billion, with expectations for continued growth in user monetization and lending profitability.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – With GCash’s stock market debut around the corner, it has another target in sight: the “5-6” lender.

That was one way executives of GCash parent Mynt tried to convince brokers and investors that the homegrown e-wallet still has plenty of room to grow during an invite-only investor briefing on October 6.

GCash already has 41.5 million monthly active users – roughly four times that of its closest competitor – but only 7.5 million are active borrowers. According to Mynt’s executives, growing the latter number is the goldmine.

“We still see a lot of opportunity to grow,” Tony Isidro, president and CEO of Mynt’s lending arm Fuse Financing, said. “We see informal lending still as the biggest competitor for us, as the biggest source of business on the B2C (business-to-customer) side.”

And it’s a sizable market. According to Frost & Sullivan research commissioned for Mynt’s prospectus, around 40% of Filipino adults with loans relied on informal lending in 2025. That includes borrowing from relatives, employers, pawnshops, and notorious 5-6 lenders, who typically lend P500 and expect P600 back. (READ: ‘5-6’ lending? Symptom of a larger problem)
GCash already has products for this market. Its GLoan Sakto offers loans as small as P100, while Borrow Load lets users borrow as little as P20 for prepaid use.

“If you look at our economic base, more than 90% are from economic class lower C2DE,” Mynt president and CEO Martha Sazon said. “The unique profile of these customers, they are like the sachet type of customers. They may not have lumpsum money at one time that they can dispense with, but they also dispense money for their every day lives.”
“There’s money in serving them,” Sazon added. (READ: [Vantage Point] Holiday dividend or market coal? What GCash could deliver by Christmas)

While GCash is best known as an e-wallet and payments service, it’s already made plenty of money from lending. Lending already accounts for 35.8% of Mynt’s adjusted revenue, compared with 63.2%, or P50.34 billion, from its core payments business. By the first half of 2026, lending’s share had grown further to 41.8%, while its total loan portfolio reached P70.5 billion. And revenue is growing too, bringing in P28.52 billion in 2025 with a two-year CAGR of 67.1%.

Now, Mynt wants to pump more money into lending. Around 60% of the net proceeds from newly issued IPO shares will go toward expanding its loan portfolio over the next one to three years, according to the company’s prospectus.

blocks.caption: On day one, rush for GCash IPO shares briefly trips up trading systems

blocks.text: But making loans is considerably riskier than processing payments, especially given GCash’s customer base. Mynt’s non-performing loan (NPL) ratio stood at 4.9% in June 2026, although it had reached as high as 9.2% in 2023 and 7.5% in 2025.

And bad loans aren’t cheap. Mynt recorded P12.62 billion in provisions for credit losses in 2025, equivalent to 44.3% of its lending revenue that year. It booked another P7.93 billion in provisions in just the first half of 2026.

“As we move closer to our vision of financial inclusion and bringing more customers from informal lending, from 5-6 to formal [lending] – which, expectedly, involves some level of risk – we do expect NPL at [a certain level],” Isidro said, saying he was comfortable with bad loans remaining within single-digit levels.

GCash is hoping that technology can help keep defaults manageable. Its AI-powered GScore uses transaction histories to assess creditworthiness, while an AI voicebot called GINA already calls borrowers with payment reminders.

Beyond lending, Mynt also wants to expand into merchant services, investments, insurance, and overseas markets. There’s plenty to keep its executives busy, especially with net income growth slowing to 7.3% year-on-year in the first half of 2026.

Mynt’s IPO has no doubt drawn strong demand, with the offer already oversubscribed. But at P6.60 per share, investors are being asked to value Mynt at roughly P442 billion, or 25.7 times its 2025 earnings. That is higher than the recent earnings multiples of fintech giants like PayPal and Brazil’s Nubank, according to Unicapital Securities.

“Mynt’s valuation already incorporates expectations of continued growth. Its premium to some established fintech peers would need to be supported by sustained user monetization, profitable lending expansion, and disciplined credit costs,” the brokerage firm said in a recent commentary.
Whether that promise can sustain investors’ enthusiasm beyond the IPO will become clearer when GCASH begins trading on Tuesday, October 20. – Rappler.com

articles.title: LTFRB vows crackdown on illegal delivery services
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) said on Monday it would strengthen its enforcement measures against illegal delivery services operating without the necessary…

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 11:57am

The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) said on Monday it would strengthen its enforcement measures against colorum delivery services (operators without the required government permits).

“We have already consolidated all the legal foundations of our campaign against colorum delivery services in order to ensure that all the cases that we would file are airtight and [provide] a high assurance of conviction,” LTFRB acting chairperson Greg Pua Jr. said in a statement.

The agency said the crackdown would target operators providing delivery services for online shopping platforms without the required permits following complaints from legitimate delivery service operators.
The LTFRB said it had consolidated its legal framework, backed by a Department of Justice legal opinion and Supreme Court decisions, to strengthen its cases against violators.
Pua warned operators engaged in illegal delivery services to stop their activities, saying the agency would not hesitate to file criminal charges against those involved.

“So this early, we warn those engaged in illegal delivery services to refrain from doing it now for your own sake because we will not hesitate to file as many criminal cases against all those involved,” he said.
The agency, however, did not identify legitimate delivery services, as well as the operators targeted by the crackdown.
The LTFRB said enforcement personnel had been reoriented to strictly impound illegally operated vehicles in accordance with constitutional requirements.
Impounded vehicles may now be released only through a court order, even if the corresponding fines have been paid, the agency said.
Penalties range from P200,000 per unit to P2 million for violations of foreign ownership laws, in addition to possible prison terms of up to 12 years under the Public Service Act.
Despite the crackdown, the LTFRB said it remained ready to assist operators seeking to legalize their businesses.
“What we can assure you is that the LTFRB is ready to assist anybody to legalize their operation. That is our commitment to those who are engaged in this illegal activity,” Pua said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Raffy Tulfo, Padilla, Alan Cayetano, Vico Sotto top OCTA 2028 senatorial survey
articles.summary: Senators Raffy Tulfo, Robin Padilla, Alan Peter Cayetano, and Pasig Mayor Vico Sotto were statistically tied at the top of a non-commissioned survey conducted by OCTA Research on preferred senatorial…

blocks.text: STATISTICAL TIE
Published October 19, 2026 11:50am

Senators Raffy Tulfo, Robin Padilla, Alan Peter Cayetano, and Pasig Mayor Vico Sotto were statistically tied at the top of a non-commissioned survey conducted by OCTA Research on preferred senatorial candidates for the 2028 elections.

In Q3 2026 Tugon ng Masa (TNM) survey conducted from September 28 to October 4, 2026, Tulfo registered the highest voting preference at 47%, followed by Padilla at 45%, Cayetano at 44%, and Sotto at 42%.
OCTA Research said the four share a rank range of first to fourth, "indicating that their relative order cannot be treated as statistically fixed."
They were followed by former senator Grace Poe and Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte with 36% voting preference each, ranking fifth to sixth, while Senator Loren Legarda registered 31%.
Others in the top were:

items: former Makati mayor Abby Binay, 29%,
Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority chief operating officer Mark Lapid, 28%,
Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero, 27%,
Education Secretary Sonny Angara, 25%,
National Anti-Poverty Commission Secretary Manny Pacquiao, 25%,
Journalist Ben Tulfo, 23%, and
Senator Jinggoy Estrada, 22%.

blocks.text: OCTA noted that their overlapping rank ranges reflected that they were “competitive” for positions within the preliminary top 12 of the hypothetical 2028 senatorial preference list.

Former senator Aquilino “Koko” Pimentel III and former chief presidential legal counsel Salvador Panelo, who both registered 20%, as well as Senator Mark Villar (19%), and former senator Gringo Honasan and labor Secretary Francis Tolentino (both 18%), also remained “within the broad statistical range covering the last available slots,” according to OCTA.

OCTA said 1,200 respondents aged 18 and above were interviewed nationwide for the survey which employed probability-based sampling. The survey has a ±3 percentage-point margin of error at the 95% confidence level.

Respondents were presented with a hypothetical list of prospective candidates and were asked the question: "I have here a list of names that may run in the May 2028 elections. If the May 2028 elections will be held today, who will you likely vote for as SENATOR? You may choose up to 12 names."

The poll firm said some individuals initially considered for inclusion in the survey were removed from the list at their request. It added that in presenting the results, names receiving less than 1% were also excluded from the published list.

It further said the exclusions should be considered when interpreting the distribution of preferences and do not imply that the published names constitute the complete or final field of potential candidates.
OCTA also stressed that the findings should not be interpreted as a forecast of the 2028 senatorial election.

"They provide only a snapshot of voter preferences during the September 28 to October 4, 2026 fieldwork period. Preferences may change substantially as political alignments, candidacies, campaign conditions, public issues, and voter information evolve. Rank ranges are reported because candidates with close percentages may be statistically tied within the survey’s margin of error," it said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Kenya pastor accused of ordering parents to starve their children to death faces verdict
articles.summary: Prosecutors say Paul Mackenzie lured the latest victims to their deaths by writing notes from his prison cell.

blocks.text: A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.
Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 children.
His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil".
Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.
Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult are facing a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.
But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder.
Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country.
Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Mackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning."
The pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him".
When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned.
"My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.

By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.
Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest in March 2023.
He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover.
"My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said.
"I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."
In the 298 pages detailing the charges against him in the current case, all of the 191 victims Mackenzie and his followers are accused of murdering are children.
Many of the bodies are still unidentified, owing to their advanced state of decomposition.
In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.

Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me".
"Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said.
"I still love him and he is still my pastor."
In contrast Dan Mackenzie believes his father should be found guilty of murder.
"He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing."
