articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon told cop friend ‘I love you’ and ‘not everything in the news is true’ after arrest, court told
articles.summary:
Accused asked fellow police officer how law enforcement would respond to reports of gunshots days before alleged murders, court hears

  • Get our

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly told a friend “I love you’” and “not everything in the news is true” a month after he was arrested over a double murder, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Dayna Schagen, who was a friend of Lamarre-Condon and is an officer with the NSW police, told his trial on Monday about a call she received in late March 2024, about a month after the alleged murders.
She initially did not pick up because it came at about 9pm from a number she did not recognise and she believed it was “rude to call after dinner time on a weeknight”.
But after the number dialled a second time, she picked up the phone and immediately recognised Lamarre-Condon’s voice.
According to her police statement, which was read to the court, he said, “Dayna, it’s Beau,” and she responded, “what the fuck, why are you calling me”.
He then said: “I just wanted to tell you that I love you and before you do anything, you need to know not everything in the news is true. It will all come out in court.”
The court heard Schagen then cut off Lamarre-Condon and said: “You killed two people, why would I ever want to speak to you again?”
She then told her boss about the phone call and made a statement to police about the incident.
Schagen did not have any role in the police investigation into the double murders as an officer.
Earlier on Monday, Schagen told the jury Lamarre-Condon had been seeing Baird on and off during 2023 and had been hoping to turn it into a relationship.
When Baird made it clear he wasn’t interested and the two broke up in April 2023, Lamarre-Condon was “still very much invested in him”, Schagen said.
“I believed that he missed him and still very much wanted to be in a relationship. It was a sore spot for the accused,” she told the court.
Baird ended things with Lamarre-Condon in November 2023.
The policeman allegedly told Schagen he had “fucked up” after Baird found out he had gone through Baird’s phone, and blocked a man Baird had been sleeping with, without his knowledge.
When she found out, Schagen told Lamarre-Condon she was “mortified he did something so stupid when they weren’t in a relationship”, the court heard.
“You’ve got no grounds to be pissed off about who he’s sleeping with, you’re not together,” she allegedly told the policeman.
after newsletter promotion
Days before the alleged murders, on 14 February 2024, Lamarre-Condon asked Schagen a “hypothetical question” about work, she told the jury.

He allegedly asked: “if you were at work and there was a job broadcast over the radio for gunshots fired, what would the police response be if someone jumped on the radio and said, ‘we’ve been flagged by a member of the public who said that children were letting fireworks off’?”
She told him police would disregard it and move on due to the sheer volume of jobs she received.
The prosecution clarified to the jury that those with a police radio can hear jobs being broadcast.
After seeing news of Baird and Davies’ disappearance, Schagen sent a message to Lamarre-Condon on 22 February 2024 that said: “are you ok? Have you spoken to him? What the fuck is going on?”
She did not receive a response, and told the court at this point she believed she had “an indication” Lamarre-Condon was potentially involved.
A day later, she saw he had been active on Facebook’s messaging service and asked him: “Where the fuck are you and what’s all this shit in the media, what’s going on?”
He opened the message but didn’t respond, the court heard.
She confirmed the conversation they had about police response to reports of gunshots were on her mind and that is why she eventually approached police.
The defence team has claimed Baird and Davies were accidentally shot in two separate struggles with the accused while he acted in “self-defence”.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv makes emergency landing after bomb threat
articles.summary: An Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna made an emergency landing in Bulgaria after a bomb threat was reported near the Bulgarian-Romanian border. A MiG-29 fighter jet escorted the plane.

image.caption: Data from flight-tracking platform, ADS-B Exchange, showed that the flight transmitted a squawk code 7700, a signal for a general emergency [FILE: October 11, 2026]Image: Graham Hughes/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: An Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna made an emergency landing in Sofia on Sunday after a bomb threat, Bulgarian authorities said.
The Airbus A320 landed safely with 51 passengers and six crew members aboard after reportedly receiving a bomb threat near the Bulgarian-Romanian border.
"During the flight, ​on the border with Romania, the crew reported a ​bomb threat signal and decided to land in Sofia extraordinarily," the Bulgarian transport ​ministry said ​in a ⁠statement.
Fighter jet escorts plane
The Airbus A320 plane was flying from Tel Aviv for Vienna but was diverted to Sofia in Bulgaria at 9:25 p.m., air tracker Flightradar24 data showed.
Data from another flight-tracking platform, ADS-B Exchange, showed that the flight transmitted a squawk code 7700, a signal for a general emergency, around the time it was diverted.
A Bulgarian MiG-29 fighter jet was scrambled to escort the aircraft.
Following the evacuation of passengers after landing, a security search of the plane was launched, Austrian Airlines said in a statement quoted by Austrian news agency APA.
"Once the search of the aircraft is complete, the passengers will be rebooked onto alternative flights as quickly as possible," the airline said.
Last month, the co-pilot of Flydubai flight was suspected of attacking his pilot in the cockpit, and attempting to hijack the plane and crash it intentionally in Israel.
Meanwhile, last week, an accidental hijacking alert from a commercial flight from the Corfu in Greece to the German city of Nuremberg caused both Croatia and Germany both to scrambled fighter jets.

articles.title: Threat forces Israel to Austria flight into emergency landing
articles.summary: The Airbus jet landed safely in Bulgaria and all passengers and crew aboard were unharmed, officials said.

blocks.text: An Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria has been forced to divert to Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat.

The Airbus A320 plane was travelling from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday night but made an emergency landing in Sofia, where passengers were evacuated, the Bulgarian transport ministry said in a statement.
The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner, the transport ministry said. No injuries have been reported and an investigation has begun.

It comes after a pilot attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight en route to Tel Aviv last month by attacking the captain, before the flight's crew and passengers overpowered him and landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
Bulgarian and Israeli media reported that a bomb threat had been made.
Austrian Airlines has confirmed a threat was made, without giving further details. A spokesperson told the AFP news agency there were 51 passengers and six crew members on board the jet.
Authorities conducted a security search of the plane after it landed in Sofia, about 30 minutes from when the alert was first raised. It was over Romania when it diverted to Sofia.
Flight tracking data showed Austrian Airlines 82 left Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday evening before landing at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia three hours later.
Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert.
The BBC has sought further comment from Lufthansa, the owner of Austrian Airlines.

articles.title: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'
articles.summary: The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a blockbuster stock market listing.

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".
The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn).

The AI industry has come under intense scrutiny recently over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and the economy. Anthropic reportedly said in its initial public offering (IPO) filing that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".
Anthropic said its proposed fund could support nonprofit organisations, and efforts to address AI's impact on the jobs market.
None of the shares held by the the fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas, it added.
Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion, the Claude developer said in a statement released on Sunday.
Technology billionaire Elon Musk responded to the announcement on social media with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." "This is what I will be doing," he added.
Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.
Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.

articles.title: Defense reporters to China embassy: Words have consequences
articles.summary: The DPC turned a familiar warning by the Chinese government back on the embassy: “Words have consequences. Every statement issued and every interview given carries consequences, whether…

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 10:22am

MANILA, Philippines — After a week of testy exchanges between Philippine officials and the Chinese Embassy in Manila, journalists covering the country’s defense beat are pushing back against being dragged into the blame game.
The Defense Press Corps of the Philippines on Sunday, October 18, rejected the Chinese Embassy in Manila's claim that Filipino reporters "exaggerate" and "take things out of context."

The group emphasized that its members quoted Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan verbatim when he said China could "easily win if it used force" against the Philippines, and that the political fallout from his words “is neither within the control nor the responsibility of journalists.”

“Some Philippine politicians and reporters have very limited comprehension about facts,” the embassy said in a Facebook post on Saturday, October 17. “But they are good at exaggeration, taking things out of context, and creating hype.”
The post did not name any journalist or news organization, or point to a specific report.

It came two days after Jing told reporters on the sidelines of a forum at Diliman College in Quezon City: “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not use force. You know, we love peace.”
The DPC, whose members cover the Department of National Defense and the Armed Forces of the Philippines, said the embassy’s target and intent was clear.

“While the embassy’s statement did not specifically name the DPC, we, along with journalists covering the West Philippine Sea and relations between the two countries, can clearly discern its disparaging intent,” the group said.
‘Words have consequences’
The DPC turned a familiar warning by the Chinese government back on the embassy.

“Words have consequences. Every statement issued and every interview given carries consequences, whether intended or not,” the group said. “We are often reminded of this principle when the Chinese side issues radio challenges within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone: ‘You bear the responsibility for whatever consequences of your actions.’”

The group said Filipino reporters regularly travel by sea and air to the West Philippine Sea, where they have witnessed and experienced Chinese aggression. At the same time, it said, they have consistently sought China’s side on water cannon attacks, collisions and new remarks from Philippine officials “in the spirit of fair play and balanced reporting.”

“It must be difficult for a country without a free press to understand the dynamics of journalistic independence and editorial judgment exercised without state control or oversight,” the DPC said. “We understand. Not all journalists are as fortunate as those who live and work in a true, albeit imperfect, democracy.”

Invoking Article 2 of the United Nations Charter, which obliges states to refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state, the group said true peace requires space for mutual understanding — “something that cannot be achieved if China continues to shoot at the messengers.”
A widening row
The embassy’s post followed days of public sparring with Philippine officials, chiefly Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.
On Wednesday, October 14, Teodoro rejected Vice President Sara Duterte’s description of the Philippines as Southeast Asia’s “troublemaker,” saying, “China alone is the troublemaker here.”
The embassy responded by branding Teodoro the “real troublemaker” and accusing him of smearing China.
Jing’s remark came the next day, when reporters asked him about Teodoro’s statement, which he called “nonsense.”

The Department of Foreign Affairs said the ambassador “had a poor choice of words that would seem to convey a thinly veiled threat of the use of force.” In turn, the embassy accused the department of “selective quotation and overinterpretation.”
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Friday, October 16, that Jing’s statement “sounds very much to me like a threat” and that he would summon the envoy.

articles.title: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai
articles.summary: Video published by several news outlets shows gunmen firing multiple shots at a car while it is moving past a crowd.

blocks.text: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff has survived a shooting in Mumbai and has not sustained any gunshot wounds, according to Indian police who are investigating the incident.
The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening, while he was in a car that was leaving a football club in the suburb of Juhu.
Several news outlets have published a video showing at least two gunmen firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of a car while it is slowly moving past a crowd.
The incident has heightened concern about the safety of public figures in India, with some killed or injured in targeted attacks in recent years.
"These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," said Eknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state, where Mumbai is located.
He paid a visit to Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor and his mother had been left "shaken" by the attack.
Police said two people were injured in the shooting, including Shroff's driver, local media reported.
This is the latest in a string of attacks on some of the country's biggest public figures in recent years.
In 2024, police in India arrested two members of a criminal gang for a gun attack targeting the home of Bollywood actor Salman Khan.
That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai.
The son of two actors, Tiger Shroff made his acting debut in 2014 with the romance film Heropanti and went on to star in several films.
He is also a football enthusiast who plays for the professional football club Mumbay FC.

articles.title: Raffy Tulfo, Padilla, Cayetano, Vico Sotto statistically tied in hypothetical 2028 Senate race
articles.summary: Sens. Raffy Tulfo, Robin Padilla, Alan Peter Cayetano and Pasig City Mayor Vico Sotto are statistically tied at the top of a hypothetical 2028 senatorial race, according to the latest Tugon ng Masa…

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 9:50am
Combination photo shows Sens. Raffy Tulfo, Robin Padilla, Alan Peter Cayetano and Pasig City Mayor Vico Sotto.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor, Philstar.com / Ian Laqui and Martin Ramos

MANILA, Philippines — Sens. Raffy Tulfo, Robin Padilla, Alan Peter Cayetano and Pasig City Mayor Vico Sotto are statistically tied at the top of a hypothetical 2028 senatorial race, according to the latest Tugon ng Masa survey by OCTA Research.

Tulfo registered a 47% voting preference, followed by Padilla with 45%, Cayetano with 44% and Sotto with 42%. The four share a rank range of first to fourth, meaning their relative positions cannot be considered statistically fixed.
Former senator Grace Poe followed with 36%, while Sen. Loren Legarda registered 31%.
Rounding out the list of prospective senatorial candidates were:

items: Sen. Raffy Tulfo — 47%
Sen. Robin Padilla — 45%
Former Senate president Alan Peter Cayetano — 44%
Pasig City Mayor Vico Sotto — 42%
Former senator Grace Poe — 36%
Sen. Loren Legarda — 31%
Makati City Mayor Abby Binay — 29%
Mark Lapid — 28%
Former Senate president Francis “Chiz” Escudero — 27%
Sen. Sonny Angara — 25%
Former senator Manny Pacquiao — 25%
Broadcaster Ben Tulfo — 23%
Sen. Jinggoy Estrada — 22%
Former Senate president Aquilino “Koko” Pimentel III — 20%
Former presidential spokesperson Salvador “Sal” Panelo — 20%
Former Sen. Mark Villar — 19%
Former senators Gringo Honasan and Francis “Tol” Tolentino — 18% each

blocks.text: OCTA's ranking placed Tulfo, Padilla, Cayetano and Sotto within the same statistical rank range of first to fourth. Poe ranked fifth to sixth, while Legarda's rank range extended from fifth to ninth.
Changes from previous survey
Compared with the second-quarter 2026 survey, Tulfo's voting preference was largely unchanged, from 47.4% to 47%, while Padilla's figure declined from 53.9% to 45%.
Cayetano's rating eased from 45.4% to 44%, while Sotto's remained steady at 42%, compared with 42% in the previous survey.
Poe's preference fell from 44.5% to 36%, while Legarda's declined from 39% to 31%. Pacquiao also recorded a lower figure, from 34.5% to 25%.
Angara's rating rose from 19.2% to 25%, while Escudero's increased from 23.2% to 27%.
OCTA warned that comparisons between survey rounds should be made carefully because the lists of names presented to respondents differed.
The poll asked respondents whom they would likely vote for as senator if the May 2028 elections were held at the time of the survey, allowing them to select up to 12 names.

"The findings should not be interpreted as a forecast of the 2028 senatorial election. They provide only a snapshot of voter preferences during the September 28 to October 4, 2026 fieldwork period," OCTA said.
"Preferences may change substantially as political alignments, candidacies, campaign conditions, public issues, and voter information evolve," it added.
The non-commissioned nationwide survey has a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

articles.title: Former Marineland beluga whale dies at California theme park
articles.summary: A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed Canadian facility.

image.caption: The entrance to SeaWorld is shown in Orlando, Fla., in January 2017. The theme park says a beluga whale that was relocated from Marineland in Ontario has died at its San Diego location. (John Raoux/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed Canadian facility.
SeaWorld San Diego says ultrasound of 9-year-old male found intestinal issues

SeaWorld San Diego said in a Facebook post that Cyprus, a nine-year-old male beluga that arrived at the park on Aug. 22, stopped eating on Friday, and an ultrasound later determined the animal's intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.
It said Cyprus had been doing well since his arrival, eating consistently and interacting with his trainers and animal care team, along with two other rescued belugas.
But it said belugas can mask discomfort or underlying concerns that are not immediately visible, adding that a full necropsy will be conducted.

Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada, and 30 of its belugas and four dolphins were transferred to other facilities in a mass relocation effort.
Why Marineland's last living belugas are on 'death watch'
SeaWorld San Diego said the other rescued belugas in its care are in stable health and remain under close monitoring as they continue to adjust to their surroundings.

"As we have indicated, this process will take a considerable amount of time. Our commitment to the health, well-being and care of these belugas, like every animal we rescue, continues," the facility said in its social media post on Sunday.
It said that after the necropsy is completed, the cause of Cyprus's death will be shared with the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

items: Everyone loved Marineland — then the tide turned. A look inside the park's final days

blocks.text: Less than two weeks ago, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago said Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga that was relocated from Marineland, died despite efforts to save her. Caspian had not been eating properly, and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels, Shedd said.
The aquarium said it performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.
A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo also died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

articles.title: Australian Greens senator denies claims of misconduct towards women
articles.summary: Jordon Steele-John says the timing of the claims is motivated by "nasty political games" within the Greens.

blocks.text: An Australian Greens senator has denied allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women and accused his party of "nasty political games", days after the claims emerged.

Last Thursday, Greens leader David Shoebridge said Senator Jordon Steele-John, 32, had taken leave from the party room after a letter from seven current and former members said he had been accused of "multiple allegations" of misconduct between 2017 and 2025.

In an online post on Sunday, the senator denied the claims and said he was not on leave. On a sexual assault claim, he said police investigating the matter had closed the case and no charges were laid.
An internal party probe has been launched into the allegations.
Steele-John, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, was first elected to the senate in Western Australia in November 2017.

In his letter responding to the claims, Steele-John said his nickname - "Feels on wheels" - initially referred to him being emotional when advocating for disability rights but had since taken on a "more sinister meaning" about his alleged mistreatment of women.

He accused Shoebridge of mishandling the matter and questioned the timing of the letter, saying "it is no coincidence" that the allegations were sent to the leader "the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection" ahead of the next federal election.

Days after the letter with the claims was sent to Shoebridge, local media reported that the party had created a 47-page dossier years earlier that listed a number of allegations against Steele-John and how to manage media coverage if they emerged.
Steele-John said the dossier was made so that the media would not "bombard" the two women at the centre of those claims and that neither woman had made a complaint.

He acknowledged the allegations against him would have "damaged" the public's trust in him and said he was "committed to rebuilding that by acting with as much transparency and accountability as I can".
Shoebridge's office confirmed that the allegations had been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.

articles.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions waivers, accuses Zelenskyy of 'prolonging war'
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump again accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. The remarks come amid renewed tensions over US policy toward Moscow including waiving…

image.caption: Trump (right) repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the US midterm election [FILE: September 22, 2026]Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trumpon Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, accusing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.

"My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," he added.
Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving broad new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine's defense.
He has also temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing supplies to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3.
Trump links Russia sanctions waiver to fuel prices ahead of midterms
Opinion polls suggest that Republicans could face significant losses in the election, as voters voice growing frustration over fuel prices that have surged since the Iran war began in late February.
Most economists believe the suspension of congressionally approved sanctions on Russia and the diesel deal with the Kremlin will do little to lower US fuel prices.
Trump also repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the midterm election.
How Trump is helping Putin
The move drew a sharp response from Kyiv and its allies, further straining relations between Trump and Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy warns Ukraine cannot prevail if US backs Russia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Sunday that Ukraine would lose its defensive battle against Russia if the United States switched sides and supported Moscow.
"If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail," Zelenskyy told NBC's 'Meet the Press' calling a withdrawal of US support "a historic mistake and big tragedy."
He said Washington had resumed sharing intelligence after it was "blocked for some period of time," adding that Ukraine had missed critical intelligence on ballistic missile attacks for three days.
Zelenskyy also criticized US restrictions affecting Ukraine's war effort, saying, "We are strategic partners," but "we cannot applaud when someone turns against Ukraine."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Trump's suspension of new sanctions on Russia, saying Trump wanted to assess their impact on the global and US economies.
Zelenskyy speaks to US envoys as Trump renews criticism

Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other's energy infrastructure, leaving thousands without power in Ukraine and setting an oil refinery ablaze near Saint Petersburg.

After the talks, Zelenskyy said "a lot depends" on the US position, adding that "this war must be brought to an end." Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly," he said, calling for the same approach from its European and US partners.
Zelenskyy said he also discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defense systems as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
A US-led push to end the war has yet to yield a breakthrough, with Trump expressing frustration at both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelenskyy accused Moscow of violating Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter. Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power, he said, while Ukrainian officials reported three deaths.
Ukraine launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.

articles.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
articles.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.

blocks.text: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.
One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.
He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.

Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.

He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.
There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.

The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."
And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.

The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.

There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.
It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.

items: If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine

blocks.text: Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.
"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.
His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.
"When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.
He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.
If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.

Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.

"You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.
Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.
He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.
"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.
"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.
Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.
"As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."
But he argued that his team's actions were justified.
"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."
Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."
But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.
Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.
Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.
Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.
Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.
"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.
To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.
Foma has the same rule for his operatives.
"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.
Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.
"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.
So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.
Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.
"You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.

Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".
But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.
Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.

"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.

Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.
Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work.
"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."
But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.
"Putin won't live forever," he said.

articles.title: Outrage after Meta suspends No Kings Instagram account during protests
articles.summary:
‘Meta owes us an explanation,’ group says as organizers fear censorship after account goes dark for several hours

The coalition leaders behind nationwide pro-democracy protests that have…

blocks.text: The coalition leaders behind nationwide pro-democracy protests that have drawn millions of Americans to the streets in recent years were frustrated when its Instagram account was temporarily shut down during its latest demonstration on Saturday.
The No Kings movement’s account went dark for several hours while protests focused on increasing early voter turnout were underway, sparking censorship fears.
Meta apologized on Saturday and blamed the account’s temporary suspension on an automated action that’s triggered “when accounts post, share or comment at very high frequencies”.
“Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone, wrote on X. “Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologize.”

“We have regained access to our accounts, but Meta still owes us an explanation,” the No Kings Coalition posted on their Instagram page, on Sunday. “Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”
In a longer statement, Stone cited the “high volume” of reading profiles, posts and hashtags in “intense bursts” on Saturday caused their AI tool to detect the activity as automated bot traffic.

“This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline. An automated re-review of the removal action an hour later recognized that shouldn’t have happened and restored the account,” Stone said. “It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account. We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error.”
Organizers remained skeptical about Meta’s explanation that high-frequency posting triggered an automated response, and said members “posted only a handful of times and livestreamed to thousands”.
Senator Bernie Sanders also expressed concerns on Sunday, on X, saying that “billionaire ownership of the media” had resulted in the suspension of the No Kings account.

Connecticut senator Chris Murphy called for an investigation into the incident in his own social media post, saying it was an indictment of Meta’s “outsized influence” on US culture and politics. “How were they not ready for the biggest day of anti-Trump protest of the campaign?” Murphy said. “An investigation is warranted, at the very least, to understand why Meta (which effectively functions these days as a private government) was unable to protect protest against Trump, while it spends so much time trying to get close to Trump.”

Despite the technical blip, hundreds of planned events continued. At the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, a band played for a few hundred people in caps and coats, many of whom were dancing and held signs saying “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!”
In Atlanta, city councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd: “The constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?”

On the streets of downtown Los Angeles, protesters carried umbrellas to protect them from the sweltering heat and a band trailed behind them on a rolling stage, the New York Times reported; the crowds cheered calls for abolishing ICE and passing California’s billionaire tax.

The No Kings movement began last summer, in response to a broad set of concerns about federal layoffs, immigration enforcement and foreign wars. The demonstrations have continued to tackle a wide range of issues, and typically lean into anti-Trump fervor.

This year’s focus on voting ahead of the midterm elections is in part due to the supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, as well as fears about Trump once again sowing chaos by baselessly calling election results into question.

No Kings organizers said they planned to recruit volunteers at Saturday’s events to mobilize in case of “election sabotage”, Leah Greenberg, a co-executive director of Indivisible, a progressive group that helps organize No Kings events, previously told the Guardian.

articles.title: Obama condemns comments by ‘border czar’ that Ilhan Omar could ‘of course’ be denaturalized
articles.summary:
Ex-president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’

Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s…
articles.byline: José Olivares and Sanya Mansoor in New York

blocks.text: Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her.
Obama wrote Sunday morning, on X, that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.”

He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs, adding: “if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her – or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.” Obama, too, has had his citizenship scrutinized by Trump, who more than a decade ago fueled false conspiracy theories that Obama was born in Kenya and therefore not eligible to be president.
Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, was asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”.
“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before.
“And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.”

Homan’s comments were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a top Trump administration official since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October.

The search of Omar’s home sparked major backlash and accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized about denaturalizing and deporting.

The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the November midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.
Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details.
“I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.”

Omar – a naturalized US citizen from Somalia – was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020.

blocks.caption: Tom Homan applauds as Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Syracuse, New York, on 9 October.  Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Obama stated in his post on X that Omar arrived in the US with her father when she was 12, and five years later, when her father became a naturalized citizen, she became one, too, because she was 17. (An 18-year-old would have had to apply for citizenship separately, he noted.)

“Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” he wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone – all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.”
In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneys accused the US justice department of potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy.

The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its on offensive on legal migration.
The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship.
As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings.
after newsletter promotion
Nonetheless, as of April, the US justice department had reportedly identified nearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate.

The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also include allegations that her ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US.
The federal government reportedly seized Omar’s phone during the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives.
Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search.

Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.
There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Even veterans at the Department of Justice expressed shock over the targeting of Omar, according to reporting by NBC News. “I was astounded to see a search of a sitting congressperson this close to an election,” said Peter Carr, a former career justice department spokesperson, NBC News reported.

“Historically, the department has been very adamant that politics plays no role in investigative decisions they make and they try very hard to avoid taking overt actions that might even have the perception of influencing an election.”
After the raid on her home, Omar posted on X that she was “ok”.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
“I will not be silenced,” Omar added.

articles.title: Times’s investigation adds more intrigue to infamous OJ Simpson case
articles.summary:
Report reveals that a shady mobser-turned-informant may have been involved in helping cover up murder

An in-depth investigation by the

blocks.text: An in-depth investigation by the New York Times is raising further questions about the high-profile OJ Simpson case, in which the former football player was accused in the 1990s of killing his ex-wife – and whether a shady mobster-turned-informant may have been involved in helping cover up the murder.

The Times’s investigation revealed that California prosecutors were unable to fully investigate whether Simpson, who was accused but not convicted of his ex-wife’s murder, may have had an accomplice at the scene of the crime.

The extensive journalistic investigation, based on previously sealed court records and interviews, adds further intrigue to the infamous Simpson case. No one was ever criminally convicted for the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.

That year, Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were found stabbed to death outside her home in Los Angeles. The American professional football player and actor, OJ Simpson, was suspected in the murder. Simpson’s prosecution gained international attention and became a media spectacle, being deemed the “trial of the century”.

Simpson was acquitted by a jury in 1995 after a lengthy trial. The Los Angeles police department, which investigated the case, had a long history of racism. Simpson’s attorneys pointed to the racist policing practices and the department’s handling of key evidence, helping them secure the acquittal. Simpson was later held liable for the deaths by a jury in a civil case.

But the New York Times has now revealed that a shady informant began revealing information about Simpson’s case towards the end of the prosecution. The informant, a wealthy mobster named Joseph Ippolito, had become a snitch after spending years on the run from the federal government.
The information Ippolito had may have been key to the trial, but it was far too late for the prosecution to include his testimony.

Ippolito, a longtime drug runner throughout the US known as Joey, came from the New Jersey underworld, where his father was a player within the DeCavalcante crime family, a major Italian American criminal organization. After a stint in prison for trafficking drugs in the east coast, he moved to California in the late 1980s and managed an Italian restaurant.

There, he was able to embed himself in the inner circles of the Los Angeles elite. Ippolito befriended Al Cowlings, a former football star and close friend of OJ Simpson. But while he spent time with Los Angeles celebrities, Ippolito continued selling and trafficking drugs.

In 1992, he was arrested by authorities again in a sting operation. But in May 1994, eight months after his sentencing, Ippolito escaped from his Florida prison. His brother helped him arrive back in Los Angeles, where he remained in hiding as a wanted fugitive.

That year, the murder of Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman took place in Los Angeles. When authorities attempted to arrest OJ Simpson, he fled. His friend Cowlings, the former football player, led the police on a widely-publicized chase through Los Angeles with Simpson in the car.

After Simpson’s arrest, officials found Ippolito’s information in Cowlings’ wallet, leading them to urgently search for the mobster-at-large. Eventually they found Ippolito and arrested him. But he decided to flip and become an informant for the US government.

As an informant, Ippolito revealed information about various drug deals throughout the country and helped federal agencies set up sting operations. But Ippolito also reportedly shared information with the government about the Los Angeles murders.
The New York Times raises three separate theories for Ippolito’s involvement in the Simpson case, which he was seemingly willing to share with authorities:
1) In one version, Ippolito told federal prosecutors he had information he learned from Cowlings about the murders, including the supposed location of the missing weapon.
2) In another version, Ippolito’s brother told a reporter with the Times that Ippolito may have been at the scene of the killings. The brother said Ippolito literally had blood on his hands.
3) And in a third version, Ippolito was prepared to help Simpson escape during the wild police chase throughout Los Angeles.

“Taken together, the material points in different directions but veers significantly from the official account that has been proffered by the police and prosecutors,” the New York Times reports. “With many of the key players now dead, it’s possible the full truth will never be known.”

Ippolito’s brother, who told the Times he had seen his brother’s hands with blood on them, later asked the publication for money and then recanted his statement to the publication. According to the report, the brother said he had been “offered a ton of money” to share his story elsewhere, likely a television program.
The extent of Ippolito’s involvement is not fully known. Authorities interviewed by the Times expressed doubts on how involved Ippolito was and the value of his information in the case.

articles.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.

blocks.text: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.

There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.

Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

articles.title: ‘Champi’ may re-intensify into super typhoon, to enter PAR Tuesday
articles.summary: Typhoon Champi has weakened as it moved west-northwestward over the sea west of Guam, but may re-intensify into a super typhoon.

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 7:15am
Satellite rendering shows Typhoon Champi taken on Oct. 18, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Typhoon Champi has weakened as it moved west-northwestward over the sea west of Guam, but may re-intensify into a super typhoon, PAGASA said Sunday night.
In its 11 p.m. bulletin on Sunday, October 18, the state weather bureau said Champi was carrying maximum sustained winds of 175 kilometers per hour near the center, with gusts of up to 215 kph.
It is moving west-northwestward at 15 kph.
The center of Champi was estimated at 1,830 kilometers east of Southeastern Luzon, outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).
Champi is expected to enter the PAR by Tuesday morning or early afternoon. Once inside the country's monitoring area, it will be given the domestic name Rosal.
Strong winds, rainfall
PAGASA said tropical cyclone wind signals may be raised over the northern and eastern portions of Northern Luzon and parts of the Bicol Region as early as Monday evening or Tuesday morning.
The highest wind signal in the current forecast scenario is Signal No. 3 or 4.
Gusty conditions may affect most parts of Luzon and the Visayas, as well as portions of Mindanao, beginning Wednesday.
The tropical cyclone is also expected to bring heavy rainfall to Extreme Northern Luzon.
Sea conditions
Moderate to rough seas may begin affecting the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon and the eastern seaboards of the Visayas and Mindanao by Tuesday.
Hazardous sea conditions, with very rough to very high seas, may affect the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon from Wednesday onward.
PAGASA said a gale warning for very rough seas will be issued on Tuesday evening or Wednesday morning.
Track, intensity
Champi will continue moving west-northwestward until it enters the PAR on Tuesday, after which it is expected to move toward Taiwan while remaining over the Philippine Sea.
The tropical cyclone is forecast to maintain its strength over the next 12 hours before re-intensifying beginning Sunday evening or Tuesday.
PAGASA said Champi may again reach super typhoon category, with further intensification possible while it moves over the Philippine Sea.
A gradual weakening trend is expected to begin on Wednesday after the tropical cyclone reaches its peak intensity.

articles.title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
articles.summary: Prime Minister Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".

blocks.text: Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta.
Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".

The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity".
"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney.
The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.
Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.
Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.

Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing.
"There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.
A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range.

"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."
Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there.
News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation.
Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".
The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said.

In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference".

Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.

Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.

The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down.
The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units.

"It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province.
STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed.

Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance.
Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said.
"I heard people screaming inside of those vehicles that will never end up being out of my mind," he recalled, saying it was "like a scene from a war movie".
Additional reporting by Lisa Lambert

articles.title: Electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals
articles.summary:
Premium paid over French counterparts has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour, analysis by lobby group finds

British steelmakers have been pushed further behind European rivals on…

blocks.text: British steelmakers have been pushed further behind European rivals on electricity costs after the US-Israeli war on Iran caused a surge in global gas prices.

The premium paid by the British industry over its French counterpart has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour (MWh), its highest level in three years, according to analysis by the lobby group UK Steel.

Energy prices have long been one of the main factors businesses cite when asked what is holding back British industry. For Andy Burnham they represent perhaps the biggest obstacle to his goal of “reindustrialising” the UK.
Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation, which is crucial for cleaner steelmaking with electric arc furnaces.

The way the market is set up means that the wholesale gas price determines the price of electricity even from other sources that cost much less to produce, such as wind or solar power, and Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz in response to Donald Trump’s bombing campaign has caused global gas prices to soar.
Electricity prices in France are mainly determined by its nuclear reactors, while in Germany heavily polluting coal still plays a large role in generation.

Comparisons with European rivals are particularly important for the UK because the EU is often the main market for British manufactured products, including about 75% of exported steel, worth about £3bn.

The gap with France had fallen in the previous three years to reach £18 a MWh last year, although it remains below the £153 reached in 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused a crisis in the global gas market. The gap with Germany this year fell slightly to about £12.

Under Keir Starmer most of the costs added by government policy to heavy industrial businesses’ electricity costs were removed last year. The main option to bring the price down further, however, would be to set up more cheap renewables – a challenge in the short term – or to directly subsidise prices.

The director general of UK Steel, Peter Brennan, said direct subsidies were the only option to help steelmakers. The lobby group has proposed a cap on prices that it estimates would cost about £51m a year. The government would pay the difference when prices go above that level, while the industry would pay the government if prices go below.

“British steelmakers are being asked to compete with one hand tied behind their backs,” Brennan said. “Despite welcome government action, our electricity prices remain vastly higher than those of our European and global competitors, and the gap with France is getting worse.
after newsletter promotion

“The government has rightly made reindustrialisation a national priority. But we cannot rebuild British manufacturing while forcing our steelmakers to pay substantially more for electricity than their competitors.”

Separately, the government announced measures on Monday to support more than 100,000 workforce opportunities in the eight key growth sectors in its industrial strategy. The “jobs plans” are intended to help young people find work, with a focus on professional and business services, the defence sector and construction.
Similar plans for financial services, clean energy and life sciences have already been announced. Plans for advanced manufacturing and the creative industries are expected to follow shortly.

A government spokesperson said: “We are tackling industry’s number one concern head-on by reducing electricity bills by up to 25% for over 10,000 manufacturing businesses, and cutting costs for hundreds of our most electricity-intensive businesses by around £1bn per year – delivering on the prime minister’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.”

articles.title: EPA quietly backtracks on claims US has phased out toxic Pfas compounds
articles.summary:
Agency changes wording on website as Texas-based firm continues manufacture of plastic container barriers

The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US…

blocks.text: The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US has phased out two of the most dangerous Pfas compounds – Pfoa and Pfos.

The EPA has found that virtually no level of exposure to either in drinking water is safe, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies Pfoa as “carcinogenic to humans” and Pfos as “possibly carcinogenic”. Still, the EPA is allowing Houston-based Inhance to produce containers from which Pfoa has been found to leach at high levels into the containers’ contents. The company makes up to 200m barriers annually for plastic containers used across the US economy.

The containers present an “ongoing serious and ongoing threat to public health,” said Kyla Bennett, a former EPA scientist who is now science policy director with the Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (Peer) non-profit.
Inhance has denied that the chemical leaches out in measurable levels, and told the Guardian in a statement that any Pfoa from its products are an “impurity”.
The EPA has written that the company is “manufacturing“ PFAS.

The “phase-out” was put in place after documents made public during landmark early 2000s litigation on DuPont’s Pfas pollution in West Virginia laid bare the ubiquitous chemicals’ dangers and serious health risks. In 2015, facing intense pressure to act, the EPA reached an agreement with eight Pfas producers to “phase out” production of Pfoa and Pfos, a similar chemical produced by 3M.

Though the agency stopped short of a ban, the “phase out” was viewed as major progress on reining in Pfas pollution. Officials often repeated the claim that the chemicals had been phased out, giving the impression that they were no longer produced or used in the US.

Last month, the EPA quietly changed wording on its website that claimed Pfoa and Pfos had been phased out.. In fact, both have been produced in the US this whole time, and at levels that independent science suggest are quite high.
The EPA site previously stated: “The manufacture and import of Pfoa has also been phased out in the United States.”
It now reads: “Quantities of Pfoa may be produced, imported, and used by companies … ”

The change was made in response to a complaint filed by Peer, which pointed out that the EPA was allowing Pfoa to be produced in the US. Under the Information Quality Act, data and information made public by federal agencies be complete and accurate.

“They were giving the false impression and saying, ‘Nothing to see here because Pfoa is not being produced in the US,’” Bennett told the Guardian. “But that was demonstrably false, and now they have admitted it.”

An epidemiological panel convened during the West Virginia DuPont case found Pfoa and Pfos likely causes cancer, heart disease, liver disease, kidney disease. The panel’s findings were the scientific basis for the phase-out.

The EPA did not immediately provide a comment to the Guardian. Inhance in its statement to The Guardian stressed that there was never a ban in place and it was not one of the eight companies that agreed to stop producing Pfoa.
The reversal underscores why phase-outs are inadequate, and the EPA needs to put in place bans, Bennett said.

“If you have a chemical and there’s no safe level of it, then why on earth would you allow it to be manufactured?” she said. “This all makes perfect sense if you understand the reality that the EPA is an arm of industry, especially under the Trump administration.”
The EPA’s reversal marks the latest twist in a six-year legal battle over Inhance’s Pfoa-infused containers.

The EPA seemed unaware that Pfas were being “manufactured” during plastic container barrier production until late 2020 testing by Peer found high levels of Pfas in pesticides stored in Inhance bins. The subsequent EPA investigation unearthed wide-scale contamination of plastic containers, prompting the agency to subpoena Inhance for information.

It publicly reminded the plastics industry that companies must submit for a safety review if they manufacture Pfoa. Inhance dismissed the agency’s evidence and claimed its containers did not leech Pfoa, but the EPA disagreed, again ordering Inhance in March 2022 to “immediately cease” production.
Two weeks later, Inhance put out a press release stating that its products did not “impart” Pfoa, and it did not cease production.

Subsequent EPA testing found the containers still contained Pfoa. Facing legal pressure from Peer, the EPA by December 2023 again ordered Inhance to stop making the containers. That ban was overturned by a federal appeals court. Peer later sued, but the case was dismissed because a federal judge ruled that the group lacked standing.
In its statement, Inhance said that it made adjustments to reduce by 90% the level of Pfoa “impurities”.

“Published peer-reviewed third-party risk assessments conclude that estimated exposure does not present an unreasonable risk to human health or the environment,” Inhance chief commercial officer Patricia van Ee wrote. “We have shared our process data with EPA throughout its review.”

The EPA appears to have given up on enforcing the phase out and legally pressuring Inhance. Still, the EPA maintained on its website that Pfoa had been phased out of production, drawing the formal complaint from Peer.
In a response dated 18 September, EPA assistant administrator for chemical safety and pollution prevention, Douglas Troutman, wrote: “In response to Peer’s request, the EPA is updating its websites.”
The update also notes that Pfos is in US production in some “limited, ongoing uses”.

“This rare touch of candor by EPA is welcome, but it does not address the free flow of toxic Pfas saturating our food, water, and soil,” Bennett said. “Now that EPA has admitted that these two legacy Pfas are still manufactured in the US, it is past time to take effective enforcement action.”

items: This article was amended on 18 October 2026 to correct Patricia van Ee’s title, and the story previously stated that Inhance manufactures plastic containers. They make the containers’ barriers.

articles.title: ‘We are beyond heartbroken’: Cindy Crawford, Rande and Kaia Gerber share tributes to Presley
articles.summary:
Family post emotional statements to Instagram a month after their son and brother died at a rehab facility

Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber have said they are “beyond heartbroken” in a…

blocks.text: Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber have said they are “beyond heartbroken” in a tribute to their “sweet beautiful” son, Presley.
Their eldest child died aged 27 at a rehab facility on 20 September, according to Los Angeles county medical examiner records. The cause of his death has not been disclosed.
Crawford and Gerber posted an emotional statement on Instagram on Sunday.
“We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother,” it said. “We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years.
“He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever. We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability.
“We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain.
“Til we meet again our sweet boy.”
The message was signed “with love forever” from Crawford and Gerber and their daughter, Kaia Gerber.
Kaia, who like her mother is a model, also expressed her support in the comments, shared a message on her own page alongside a carousel of images and videos of herself with Presley.
In a letter addressed to her brother, she wrote: “Prez, I don’t have the words. Maybe the tiny mercy is that we didn’t need them all along.”
She wrote that she had “none of the answers” and could not articulate the “magnitude” of losing her brother.
“You know how much I loved being your sister. It has always been, and will forever be, my favourite thing about myself.”
The letter described her older brother as “inherently good” and her “ultimate teacher”, recounting childhood memories as she reflected on her grief.

“I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you,” Kaia she. “How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can’t reach for you in. I don’t know how to do that yet.”
She concluded: “My best buddy, my great protector, the hardest I’ve ever laughed and the one true love of my life. You lit all of my candles and took all of my monsters away, and I love you.”
The post was set to the song First I Was by Jake Minch, which Kaia described as “the last thing we talked about”.
The actors Taylor Lautner and Patrick Schwarzenegger, the singer Suki Waterhouse and the socialite Paris Hilton commented on the post.
